articles.title: Pope Leo draws 2.5 million in Buenos Aires, renews warning over Milei's austerity
articles.summary: An estimated 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care…

image.caption: Argentina had not hosted a papal visit since 1987, despite being the homeland of Leo's predecessor, FrancisImage: Andrew Medichini/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: An estimated 2.5 million people attended Pope Leo XIV's open-air mass in Buenos Aires on Monday, according to local authorities, making the event the largest gathering of his papacy so far.

Crowds stretched for miles along Avenida del Libertador in Argentina's capital, with the faithful waving Vatican flags and chanting "Long live Pope Leo!" as the US-born pope passed in an open-top popemobile.
"It fills my heart with joy to celebrate... with you," Leo said in his sermon.

The pope also reinforced an appeal to President Javier Milei to protect vulnerable Argentines, visiting a disability care home struggling with the government's cuts to health care and social services.
What did Pope Leo say about Milei's spending cuts?
Before the mass, Leo visited the Cottolengo Don Orione care center in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, which houses more than 400 people with disabilities.
He told residents their lives were a blessing rather than a burden, and challenged the idea that economic success alone measures a country's achievements.
"A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

blocks.caption: Some worshippers had camped overnight to secure a place at Argentina's first papal massImage: Andrew Medichini/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The remarks followed his appeal Sunday, at a reception attended by Milei, for economic growth to benefit people facing the greatest difficulties. He also urged leaders to choose their words carefully and recognize the limits of their power.

Milei became the president of Argentina some three years ago, Since then, his government has cut disability services and resisted implementing a law increasing funding for care, despite Congress overriding Milei's veto in 2025. The Senate is due to consider next year's disability funding in the coming days.
Argentina declares national holiday over Pope Leo's visit
Some worshippers camped overnight to secure a place near the Monumento a los Espanoles, where Pope John Paul II celebrated Argentina's last papal mass in 1987.
Monday was declared a national holiday to allow people to attend. President Milei and his sister Karina were among those present.
Pope's message for Milei
In his sermon, Leo spoke of families facing unstable employment, violence and addiction, while describing them as a pillar of society.
Where is the pope traveling next?
The visit is Argentina's first by a pope in nearly four decades. Leo's predecessor Francis, despite being born in Argentina, never returned to his homeland during his papacy.
Leo, 71, visited Uruguay before arriving in Argentina on Sunday. He is due to travel to Peru on Wednesday and return to Rome on November 17.
The first US-born pope spent decades in Peru as a missionary and bishop. The Vatican has described his South American tour as a "homecoming."
The demanding trip comes less than a month after surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.

articles.title: Witnesses recount struggle to save people buried in ‘horrifying’ Gaza landslide
articles.summary:
High winds and heavy train triggered collapse of sand bank overlooking camp for displaced families

Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke

blocks.text: Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a landslide triggered by high winds and heavy rain in Gaza.
A sand bank overlooking a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah collapsed on Sunday, killing five people and crushing at least three tents.

“It was a horrifying sight,” said Abdul Karim al-Sahhar, 30, originally from Izbat Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza. “We saw people buried beneath the sand and rocks. None of them was moving or making a sound. Even the tent had disappeared completely. There was no trace of it left.”
Among the casualties was an eight-year-old, a six-year-old and their mother.

Sahhar, whose own shelter was badly damaged in the landslide, said the children’s father was outside the family tent and so survived. “One of his children had called him to come and eat with them,” he said. “He was a little late returning, and then the collapse happened.

“The father started shouting: ‘Save my children! Save my children!’ People came and started digging [but] there was a huge boulder on top of the victims. The young men had to break it into pieces so they could reach the people buried underneath.”

Abu Darbali, another witness, said the collapse of the embankment sounded like an explosion. “We found that three tents were covered completely after the mountain collapsed on top of them,” he told Reuters. “People were under the rubble and we couldn’t see them.”
Video posted to social media showed residents using hammers to break large rocks and others removing sand with shovels, searching for people trapped underneath using flashlights.

blocks.caption: Palestinians remove sand at the site of the deadly sand bank collapse. Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: The UN said more than 26,000 households had reported damage to shelters or belongings after the weekend’s rainstorms.

The vast majority of Gaza’s population of 2.3 million live in tent encampments or the ruins of bombed-out buildings, ‌with reconstruction yet to begin after Israel’s relentless two-year military assault launched after the Hamas attacks on southern Israel in October 2023.

“The collapse [this weekend] was waiting to happen. [Gaza] is extremely overcrowded. People are just trying to find a place wherever,” said Toby Fricker, a spokesperson for Unicef, which has been working to prevent similar tragedies and improve drainage in camps for the displaced.

In a statement, the Hamas-run government media office said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains. It also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some critical, in various areas of the tiny territory.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made. Negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops, which control about two-thirds of the territory ‌from which residents have been ordered to leave.
Israel says no reconstruction can happen before Hamas is disarmed.

Sahhar said he and his family were now homeless. “My tent and everything I own are now buried under the sand. My mattress, household utensils and all my belongings – everything was buried. I could not retrieve anything,” he said.

blocks.caption: Palestinians inspect tents buried under rocks following the collapse of a large sandstone slab. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: Mustafa Qazzaat, a member of the Gaza City council, said Israel had not allowed prefabricated homes to shelter the displaced since the truce was announced, and only permitted the entry of limited numbers of tents.
Many so-called “dual use” items remain restricted, such as metal tent poles. Humanitarian workers said they instead had used wooden poles fashioned from palettes used to transport food.

Cogat, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees aid to Gaza, said over 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks containing tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothinghad reached Gaza, as well as convoys carrying supplies of fuel and engine oil to power pumping facilities and other humanitarian installations.

Earlier this year, an assessment compiled by shelter specialists in Gaza revealed that thousands of tents supplied by China, Egypt and Saudi Arabia to shelter displaced Palestinians offered only limited protection against rain and wind.

articles.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
articles.summary: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

blocks.text: A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.
"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.

The effort will likely fail, given Republicans will remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says he wants to push President Donald Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch an impeachment process.
Hegseth, who will hold a news conference on Tuesday about Massie's move, said he was not concerned.
"We're not worried about that," Hegseth said when asked by reporters about the impending resolution on Monday, adding he would hold a news conference Tuesday morning "on that very topic".
Hegseth's last news conference was in May.
Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, is among the few Republicans who have been critical of Trump and the war that started earlier in this year in Iran.

The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and is now pressing for a vote in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said his push to rid the administration of Hegseth is meant to prevent a Democrat spectacle next year.

"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."
"President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," he also said.

Impeaching a cabinet secretary is very rare. The impeachment must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not agree on either one.

Once Massie introduces his resolution - expected later on Monday - Speaker of the House Mike Johnson must schedule a time to consider it within two days. Along with voting on the resolution directly, the House has the option to vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.

Massie will likely have the support of the Democrats in the House, with that party's leader, Hakeem Jeffries, saying on Sunday that he is a "hard yes" on impeachment. But Massie would still need to win over members of his own party.
The House has passed a War Powers resolution - a measure that seeks to halt Trump from taking further military action in Iran - multiple times this year, with Massie's support.
But Massie's disagreement with Hegseth also goes beyond Iran, he said in the statement.
He has accused Hegseth of intimidating critics of the Trump administration, kidnapping foreign leaders and ignoring congressional war powers resolutions.

articles.title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.summary: The share price dropped wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the value of Nvidia.

blocks.text: Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 6% on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying "allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
After the investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened on a positive note on Monday after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.

But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so central to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but Huang decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.

Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.

Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

articles.title: Ford says protesters against changes to Ontario’s student aid program should be ‘thanking the government’

blocks.text: Toronto

Ontario Premier Doug Ford called students who protested Ontario Student Assistance Program changes and tuition hikes "naive" on Monday — likening them to "sheep" who blindly follow "looney tunes" on social media.
Post-secondary students across Ontario walked out of classes to protest grant cuts, tuition hikes
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 09, 2026 12:37 PM EST | Last Updated: 40 minutes ago
Ford: Students protesting OSAP cuts should be 'thanking the government'

Ontario Premier Doug Ford called students who protested Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) changes and tuition hikes "naive" on Monday — likening them to "sheep" who blindly follow what "looney tunes" post on social media.

Ford was speaking at an unrelated news conference Monday morning when he was asked about last week's "Hands Off Our Education!" campaign protests, which took place on several campuses across Ontario, including York University, the University of Guelph, Trent University and University of Windsor.

The protests came after the province lifted a seven-year tuition freeze earlier in the year, and announced changes to OSAP in February, citing "unsustainable" costs, that cut the amount of grant funding students could receive through the program.
"These kids are so naive," he said. "They should be … thanking the government for just investing."
Ford went on to say the post-secondary students should be focused on "getting a job of the future," in fields like STEM and health care.
"They read the social media and half the people on social media [are] a bunch of looney tunes," he said. "They all run out like sheep.
"Give your head a shake, kids."

items: Post-secondary students across Ontario walk out of classrooms to protest OSAP changes, tuition hike
Ford says he feels 'badly' for students caught up in his government's career college OSAP pause

blocks.text: Instead of walking out, students should remain in class, Ford said, adding Canada has "incredible students."

"The ones that study, you're going to be successful because the number one thing you need when you leave university or college is a good paying job," he said. "We have the brightest students in the world as far as I'm concerned."

articles.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 16 people
articles.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.

blocks.text: At least 16 people have died and 13 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas plant, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.
The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.
Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.
Eyewitnesses said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.
In a statement, the company said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.
Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people are believed to be still under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued. He also said two of the injured were in a serious condition.
At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.
The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

articles.title: Mahmood’s ICE-style immigration raid agency accused of ‘fishing expeditions’
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Almost two-thirds of visits lead to no arrests and nearly three-quarters are conducted without a warrant

Shabana Mahmood’s ICE-style raid agency has been accused of engaging in…

blocks.text: Shabana Mahmood’s ICE-style raid agency has been accused of engaging in “fishing expeditions” after figures disclosed that almost two-thirds of enforcement visits result in no arrests and nearly three-quarters are conducted without a warrant.
The home secretary has hailed the expanded use of immigration enforcement teams, and claimed they will help to secure the UK’s borders by removing a key incentive for irregular migration.

Under her leadership, raids have targeted establishments associated with informal “black market” work such as nail bars, car washes, barbers, takeaways, construction sites and warehouses, as well as people’s homes.
They have been accompanied by videos posted on TikTok showing arrests of people working without authorisation being tackled to the ground by enforcement officers and locked in the back of vans.
Freedom of information requests, however, show that:

items: There were 23,538 immigration enforcement engagements such as workplace raids, home raids and spot checks in 2025 – or 60 a day. Of these, 15,578, or 66.1%, resulted in no arrests.
Only 25.81% of visits where a premises was accessed used a warrant. Critics say this suggests the Home Office is launching “fishing expeditions” based on weak intelligence.
Nearly nine out of 10 (89%) of leads alleging “immigration crime” in 2025 came from the public or from Crimestoppers, a charity that collects anonymous tip-offs. Around 2% came from the police.

blocks.text: The Home Office vigorously disputed claims that the agency launches “fishing expeditions”, claiming that intelligence is thoroughly examined before launching an immigration raid.
The findings have emerged after inquiries by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the Guardian amid growing concerns about the effect on innocent workers and businesses.

blocks.caption: The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood.  Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Officers from immigration enforcement swooped from unmarked vans last month on Sultanz, an Indian restaurant in Camborne, Cornwall, as customers sat down to eat.
The restaurant’s owner, Samsu Ali, said it felt as if his six-year-old business was being invaded. “As soon as they parked … everyone runs to the kitchen, front door, back door, everywhere,” he said.
The officers had no warrant, he said. Once in, they asked every worker for their details.
Nanu Mia, a Bangladeshi employee who had been packing meals for collection, gave his details to the officers, but they struggled to understand him.
Mia was handcuffed, arrested and marched to a van. He was de-arrested and released after his sister rushed to the restaurant with his ID card, which helped to prove that he was allowed to work.
The restaurant’s customer numbers have fallen steeply since the raid despite being cleared of any immigration breaches, Ali said.

In a local Facebook group, a question about the incident resulted in racist and threatening comments. One person wrote: “People with somewhat darker skin are literally taking over our community and causing a lot of unrest.”
The comments left Ali struggling to sleep. “They don’t understand how much money and time I have spent in the last six years,” he said.
If immigration enforcement officers do not have a warrant, they can rely on other powers to enter the premises.
after newsletter promotion

They can enter licensed premises – a restaurant, pub, hotel, cafe or any business that sells alcohol or provides late-night hot food – without a warrant under section 179 of the Licensing Act 2003. Or, in most cases – more than 12,000 last year – they can ask for the consent of the tenant, manager or owner.
When using this power, officers are meant to inform the person of their rights, including the fact that they are free to revoke their consent at any time.

Once inside, officers have the power to question individuals about their immigration status. They can ask to see identity documents. They are not supposed to detain someone without reasonable suspicion that the person is an immigration offender.

Kevin Barker, a former immigration officer who now works with businesses wrongly accused of employing people who do not have the right to work in the UK, said raids are often “fishing expeditions” based on tenuous tipoffs.
“You’re not allowed to apply for a search warrant if the intelligence you’ve got is old or an anonymous allegation that can’t be corroborated … but it doesn’t stop them,” he said.
Mothin Ali, the deputy leader of the Green party, said the findings were alarming and called on the government to “end these unjustified raids and protect people’s rights”.
“This is racist harassment dressed up as immigration enforcement,” he said.
“The falling use of warrants is deeply concerning and raises serious questions about the legality of these operations. Britain must not import Trump’s ICE playbook.”

Arrests of people from abroad working illegally in the UK have doubled since Labour has been in government. The Home Office said in August that more than 17,000 had been made since July 2024, a 122% increase on the previous two years, with a record number of immigration raids and arrests in 2026.
Opposition parties have claimed that opportunities to work illegally in the UK act as a pull factor for migrants, encouraging people to cross the Channel in small boats.

articles.title: Top U.S. hedge fund executive named CEO of Canada's new sovereign wealth fund
articles.summary: A top executive at one of the world's largest hedge funds is leaving her job in the U.S. to become the CEO of one of the Carney government's hallmark projects.

image.caption: Karen Karniol-Tambour is the first CEO of the Canada Strong Fund, the federal government announced on Monday. (Jeenah Moon/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New
A top executive at one of the world's largest hedge funds is leaving her job in the U.S. to become the CEO of one of the Carney government's hallmark projects.
Karen Karniol-Tambour 'returns to Canada as a leading figure in global finance': PMO
On Monday, the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) announced that Karen Karniol-Tambour will become the CEO of Canada's nascent sovereign wealth fund.
A news release from the PMO said Karniol-Tambour has Canadian citizenship, though public records indicate she was born in Israel and has spent her professional career in the United States.
Her LinkedIn page says she has been at Bridgewater Associates for more than 20 years and rose to be co-chief investment officer. She graduated from Princeton University in 2006.

items: Carney's bet on economic growth — and the risks that come with it
Mark Carney's quiet revolution rests on investment and affordability

blocks.text: The financial magazine Barron's has named Karniol-Tambour in its list of the 100 most influential women in U.S. finance for the last seven years. She was also featured by Forbes.

At the helm of the new sovereign wealth fund, she will be tasked with identifying and investing in domestic projects with the goal of generating returns for investors and reinvesting them in new Canadian projects.

The federal government announced plans to create the fund, which it is calling the Canada Strong Fund, last spring. It has earmarked $25 billion in seed funding and committed to putting commercial asset revenue into the fund. Its goal is to finance "nation-building" projects while allowing Canadians to benefit from the returns.

The fund will also include a "retail" element for ordinary Canadians to be able to buy in directly. Last week's federal budget said those investments will take the form of notes similar to savings bonds, but details on when or how that will roll out haven't been announced.

"Under Ms. Karniol-Tambour’s leadership, the Canada Strong Fund will be professionally managed, operating at arm's length from the government, with its own board of directors," said the Prime Minister's Office.
"Together, the fund and its retail offering will create a new model of Canadian ownership, helping build national wealth while ensuring more Canadians share in the benefits of economic growth."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records
articles.summary: Exclusive: WhatsApp messages show firm pressuring Zubir Ahmed MP to help bring sensitive data into its platform

blocks.text: Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients.

The US company, co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, used a direct WhatsApp channel to argue that “the logic of joining up primary and secondary [care] data is unarguable” and said its software was “ideal” for the job. The push came in February this year despite GP data being expressly ruled out of scope of Palantir’s existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform (FDP), which it says has helped cut surgery waiting times and discharge delays.

The messages – which were obtained under the Freedom of Information Act by Foxglove, a tech equity campaign group, and shared with the Guardian – appear to be between Palantir’s UK boss, Louis Mosley, and the former health minister Zubir Ahmed. They span several months from July 2025 to March 2026.

In the messages and a briefing document, Palantir urged Ahmed to “get out ahead of” likely “political” opposition from doctors and vocal critics of Palantir, such as the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, and Your Party, led by Jeremy Corbyn and Zarah Sultana. The firm also told Ahmed: “The FDP is already delivering very strong results – but will deliver even more benefits faster with the right ministerial sponsorship.”

Groups representing doctors and patients, including the British Medical Association, have opposed the integration of GP data into Palantir’s FDP, arguing there is a lack of trust in the company, which also works for the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). When Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government announced the deal with Palantir three years ago, it said: “GP data will not be part of the national platform.”

The lobbying emerges after it was reported last week that ministers were unlikely to end Palantir’s NHS data management contract imminently, defying campaigners and two House of Commons committees that wanted the company to be forced out as soon as spring. The Financial Times reporting, which suggested the Palantir contract will be extended, came amid concerns that removing the firm’s AI technology would be disruptive without an alternative lined up. The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, last week told parliament the review was ongoing, but said there was “a huge long-term benefit to using the NHS to develop UK sovereign AI” – a sign that the government may seek a UK replacement for Palantir when the contract reaches its next end point in 2029. Bloomberg also reported that Tom Watson, a Labour peer hired as a full-time lobbyist by Palantir in September, recently wrote to Cooper urging her to keep the contract going, saying: “I want to ensure that Palantir UK rises to meet the government’s new social-value tests and helps build Britain’s sovereign technological capability.”

The WhatsApp logs released under the FoI Act show Palantir telling Ahmed that the benefits to the health system of applying its software – known as Foundry – to GP data could include “faster access to GPs … more effective and targeted management of frail patients, and more effective preventative care”. It also said Palantir’s software platform would “maintain local control of data”.

The Palantir executive’s name is redacted in the documents released by the department of health, but Palantir did not deny it was Mosley. In one message, the minister praises a performance on a BBC1 Sunday politics programme, just after Mosley had appeared.
“Great work [on] Kuenssberg btw,” Ahmed said.

The Palantir executive advised the minister that “the politics [of using GP data] is not straightforward – the previous government ruled GP data out of scope when announcing the FDP. So, as this moves forward, it will be one to get ahead of and explain, otherwise the opponents described above will make hay with it.”
Donald Campbell, director of advocacy at Foxglove, said the WhatsApps showed Palantir “lobbying to hoover up yet more of the British public’s sensitive personal data”.
“It is appalling to see Palantir pressuring the minister to bring GP records into its platform, despite pledges from the government in 2023 that this would not happen,” Campbell said.
The correspondence “shows they knew just how sensitive this was” and it was “telling [that] they made this argument privately, via privileged access to the government”, he added.

Tom Dolphin, chair of the BMA council, raised concerns about “scope creep” with Palantir potentially accessing identifiable personal data in the GP record that could “undermine patient trust and threaten the doctor-patient relationship”.
“Patients must be able to seek care without worrying which operators might have access to duplicates of their personal information,” he said.

Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytical Officers Network, said: “Palantir appears to be bidding to stretch the scope of its work for NHS England in a way that goes beyond statements from ministers and NHS leaders that GP data was not in the scope of the FDP contract and would require legislative change … As two separate select committees have noted, public trust and transparency is essential to us being able to realise the fantastic opportunities that technology and data offer.”

Palantir said: “We’ve long argued that data sharing can improve the NHS, for patients and taxpayers, and that our software helps different NHS organisations to do that, while ensuring they maintain full local control over their data. We’ve also always been clear that it is for the government to decide how they roll the software out. These exchanges reflect both of those points”.
The Department of Health and Social Care declined to comment.

articles.title: Reform UK councillor in Sunderland handed community order after racist ‘joke’ about Nigerians
articles.summary:
Glenn Gibbins sentenced to 150 hours of unpaid work by South Tyneside magistrates over 2024 Facebook post

A Reform party councillor who claimed racist comments about Nigerians were no more…
articles.byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent

blocks.text: A Reform party councillor who claimed racist comments about Nigerians were no more than a “bit of fun” has been handed a community order for posting grossly offensive material.
Glenn Gibbins, who was voted on to Sunderland council in May, wrote on Facebook in March 2024: “Carnt believe the amount of nigerians in town … should melt them all down and fill in the pot holes!!”

At a trial before a district judge on Monday, Gibbins, 66, said it was meant to be no more than “cheeky”, “naughty” and “tongue in cheek”. He said the post was not meant to be taken literally. “It was just a bit of fun.”
It was agreed at South Tyneside magistrates court in South Shields that the social media post was offensive – the question was whether it was grossly offensive.
District judge Zoe Passfield ruled that the post breached the Malicious Communications Act and was grossly offensive.
She said Gibbins “intention was to be grossly offensive to Nigerians as a result of his displeasure at the number of them in the city.”
Gibbins has been sentenced to a 12-month community order with 150 hours of unpaid work. Adam King defending, said they would be appealing against the decision to the crown court.
Prosecutor Emma Dowling said Gibbins’ post was talking about “exterminating” a group of people. “To say that it’s not to be taken seriously is to disregard history,” she said.
“The comment about melting them down conjures up despicable images.”
Godwin Ejeh, the leader of the Nigerian community in Sunderland, was called as a witness and recalled how he called an emergency meeting of Nigerians after the post came to light.

The mood of the meeting was “chaotic”, he said because of the “level of distress”. People were concerned for their safety and the safety of their children. People wanted an apology so decided a protest should take place outside city hall.
Ejeh, a Lib Dem council candidate in May, said the comments should never have been made. “We are talking about humans. It’s not something people should play with.”
Gibbins, who ran a mobile personalised gifts and T-shirt kiosk in a Sunderland shopping centre, said he would not have described himself as a political person before this year.
He said he thought he was approached by Reform in March to run as a councillor because of a T-shirt with Nigel Farage on it on a mannequin on his stall.

He had been asked to print the T-shirt by someone drinking all day in a nearby pub. That person was “clearly intoxicated”, Gibbins said, and forgot to pick up the T-shirt, so he put it on the mannequin.

When he got a call from Reform asking if he would run as a councillor he saw it as a way of getting some income during the normal summer lull for his business. “They explained they were looking for a candidate. I didn’t even know councillors got paid. I thought it would tide me over.”
King said his client’s social media post was not politically motivated. “Reform would do well to pay more attention to the people they put forward for election,” he said.

Gibbins made the post after a couple of beers and said they were not his words. He said he had been trying to repost something he read but failed so typed in the words himself. About six friends responded with laughter, thumbs up and heart emojis.
King said it was a “stupid, unfunny joke. We come across stupid, unfunny jokes all the time.”

He pointed to jokes by professional comedians that had not resulted in criminal proceedings, namely Jo Brand in 2019 on the BBC, making a joke about throwing battery acid on Nigel Farage; and Jimmy Carr when he made a joke about the Holocaust and Gypsies on his Netflix special.
King said courts in the UK had also asserted the importance of free speech in “full-throttled, uncompromising terms”.
Gibbins said he had been suspended by Reform, then reinstated, but was now suspended again.

articles.title: Air pollution soars as fog traps emissions in England’s urban areas
articles.summary:
Particles from fireworks and bonfires likely to have contributed to levels well above WHO’s daily guideline

Air pollution soared to “very high” levels across urban parts of England on Monday…

blocks.text: Air pollution soared to “very high” levels across urban parts of England on Monday as still, foggy weather kept emissions trapped after a weekend of fireworks and bonfires.

Government monitoring showed 11 sites, mainly in London and Greater Manchester, reached the highest band on its 10-point index for particulate matter in the 24 hours to 10am. A further 27 sites recorded “high” levels across the capital, the north-west, the Midlands, Yorkshire and the east of England.

The worst reading was in Hillingdon, west London, where fine particles (PM2.5) peaked at a 24-hour average of 129 micrograms per cubic metre, more than eight times the World Health Organization’s daily guideline. In the north-west, Manchester Piccadilly, Wigan, Blackburn, Preston and Rochdale all reached the “very high” band.
Particulate matter consists of tiny solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in the air. Exposure is linked to heart and lung disease and cancer.
Jane Burston, the CEO of the Clean Air Fund, said although monitoring networks could not determine where pollution came from, it was highly likely the pollution was from autumn celebrations.

“It’s a combination of the weather, which has been foggy and not windy at all, and then the fireworks and bonfires and Diwali,” she said. “What it means is the wind doesn’t blow the pollution away and the fog keeps it trapped down in the same place.
“If you’ve got asthma or a lung condition, you absolutely will not have wanted to go outside this morning or yesterday – it can bring on asthma attacks, coughing and wheezing.
“But for everybody, it’s dangerous. People in some of the worst-affected areas are breathing particulate matter concentrations five to 10 times above normal annual levels,” she added.

Burston called for better pollution forecasts, more widely accessible health alerts and stronger action to reduce emissions from wood burning and transport. “If we had air quality at a much safer lower level all year round, then on nights like Bonfire Night, the extra pollution is less likely to push us to extreme levels,” she said.

Larissa Lockwood, the director of campaigns at Global Action Plan, said the high pollution levels were “not surprising at a time of year when people are lighting log burners, having bonfires and lighting fireworks. On top of the normal levels from transport and industry, we see higher levels of air pollution and they’re then unable to disperse because they’re trapped by the fog.”

Domestic burning and transport are the biggest sources of particulate pollution, she said. Lockwood called for a public health campaign on air pollution and “burn alerts”, asking people in towns and cities not to use wood burners when levels are high.
after newsletter promotion
“We need to phase out non-essential burning in our towns and cities so that we don’t experience these unhealthy air pollution levels,” she added.

A spokesperson for the mayor of London said: “On the advice of forecasters at Imperial College London, we’ve issued a high air pollution alert for Tuesday 10 November. Monitoring data show that pollution levels rose sharply across London from Friday to Sunday and remained elevated into Monday morning.”

A Clean Air Greater Manchester spokesperson said: “Higher particulate pollution levels occur each year around Bonfire Night, when fireworks and bonfires add particulate matter to the air. This year, weather conditions are also an important factor, with light winds and fog creating conditions in which pollution from a range of sources can accumulate near ground level. The latest information and health advice provided by Defra is available online.”
The government has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Donnie Dunagan, original voice of Disney’s Bambi and triple Purple Heart marine, dies aged 92
articles.summary:
Dunagan was six when he voiced the young deer in the classic cartoon, with an assistant director instructing him to pretend his own mother had died

Donnie Dunagan, who voiced Bambi in the…

blocks.text: Donnie Dunagan, who voiced Bambi in the Walt Disney classic, as well as playing the son of Frankenstein opposite Basil Rathbone and Boris Karloff, has died aged 92.

Dunagan was six when he was chosen to provide the voice of the young deer in the animation’s most heartbreaking chapter. He recalled the experience in the recording booth as easy and relaxed, with rudimentary technology and notes from an assistant director instructing him to pretend his own mother had died when voicing Bambi’s reaction to his mother being killed by a hunter.

blocks.caption: Heartbreaking … Dunagan was six when he provided Bambi’s voice Photograph: John Davidson/The Guardian

blocks.text: The actor recalled that Bambi’s mother originally dies on screen, but Disney altered this in the edit. Nonetheless, Dunagan received considerable hate mail from the hunting community afterwards.

Bambi, whose release was delayed in the wake of the attack on Pearl Harbor, ended up being Dunagan’s final film. He began his career on horror films Son of Frankenstein and Tower of London, playing the curly blond-haired son of Rathbone’s Dr Frankenstein, as well as featuring in films such as Mother Carey’s Chickens, The Forgotten Woman, Vigil in the Night and Meet the Chump.
He recalled often playing checkers with Karloff on set, while the latter was in full makeup dressed as the monster.

After college, Dunagan joined the military in 1952 where he spent 25 years and for which he was awarded a bronze star and three Purple Hearts for bravery. He never disclosed his early career to his comrades, but said that “one of the biggest regrets of my life is that I didn’t have the courage to tell my close personal friends in the Marine Corps that I had been a part of the wonderful work of Mr Disney”.

In 2015, he reflected on the experience by calling it “pure joy that both children and 80-year-olds can enjoy the film together. I could be working in the White House and children couldn’t care less. But let someone say, ‘that dude over there was the face or voice of Bambi’, and I am an immediate adopted grandfather to them. That is just an unmatchable joy, and a real responsibility.”

articles.title: High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate negotiator tells Cop31
articles.summary:
Simon Stiell makes opening address at summit in Turkey, where talks are under way about speeding up shift to electrification

A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a…
articles.byline: Graham Readfearn,Oliver Milman and Fiona Harvey in Antalya, Turkey

blocks.text: A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet, the UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, told the opening plenary of critical UN climate talks in Turkey.

Stiell joined Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an optimistic alternative to a planet still tied to oil, coal and gas.

Inside the tight security of the opening plenary on Monday, delegates from almost 200 countries watched a stirring short film with scenes of fire, flood and storms that proclaimed: “It’s time to reconnect with the planet we have grown apart from.”

Turkey said it expected 100,000 visitors, including national delegations, to attend the two-week talks, including at least 95 heads of state. A global leaders summit is scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday. But the talks are under increased pressure to deliver, after growing dissatisfaction with the snail’s pace of results.

blocks.caption: Activists take part in a fossil of the day demonstration on the opening day of the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya on Monday. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters

blocks.text: The talks are opening as a historic El Niño builds in the tropical Pacific and less than two months after a glacier collapse set off catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet, wiping away villages and killing at least 1,459 people, with thousands more still missing. Climate scientists confirmed this year that global heating would reach at least 1.8C – beyond the 1.5C temperature goal that countries promised to aim for at talks in Paris in 2015.

Last week Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told the Guardian that although he still had faith in the negotiating process, “the fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast … and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

And in a statement the UN secretary general, António Guterres, urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.

Stiell also said: “The urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth,” adding that it was vulnerable communities paying the price and frustration at a lack of fairness was palpable.

US President Donald Trump’s war with Iran and the disruption of the key strait of Hormuz supply route for oil pushed up petrol prices around the world by 50%, raising inflation and slowing economic growth.
Stiell told delegates this “fossil fuel cost chaos” had “delivered a global shock wave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer”.

Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, the president of the negotiations, said in a speech that will set the tone for the talks that although the 1.5C Paris target will be overshot “we can return … if we work together and act with urgency, solidarity and resolve”.

blocks.caption: Chris Bowen at the Cop31 opening ceremony. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters

blocks.text: With fists clenched in the final moments of a speech, Bowen urged delegates to show future generations that this generation was “equal to the challenge” and to “rise to this moment together”.

The countries pushing for the greatest action at Cop31 have stressed the 1.5C temperature rise limit can’t be abandoned and called for accelerated steps to provide finance to the places most vulnerable to climate impacts. The so-called high-ambition coalition said it has 20 country members pushing for major progress in Antalya.
“That limit is in serious danger but overshoot should never become an excuse for inaction, every fraction of a degree matters,” said Jess Gasper, an environmental official for the Marshall Islands.
after newsletter promotion
“We must limit overshoot and return to a safe temperature as quickly as possible.”
Gasper said it took eight years to get international finance to build a single sea wall to help protect the Marshall Islands, a Pacific island nation acutely threatened by sea level rise.
“That example shows we need that money to adapt,” he said. “I refuse to accept that we experience displacement because the world fails to act.”

The talks began without a fight over the agenda, which was considered by many to be a good sign. There was confidence among delegates that a final decision from Cop31 would include reference to a new voluntary electrification goal being championed by the host, Turkey, and the president of the negotiations, Australia.
Bowen said he had spoken to countries around the globe that were represented at the talks and there was “enormous momentum” among them for electrification.
The goal, he said, was to raise the percentage of final energy consumption coming from electricity from the current one-fifth to one-third in the next ten years.

Dr Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency, said: “I have talked with many governments and I see there is a great appetite for many countries to be part of this historic decision [in Antalya].”
He told the Guardian: “The important thing is that we are entering the age of electricity and this [electrification goal] would give an extra boost to that movement.”

Countries agreed at the 2023 climate summit to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030. Birol said if countries endorsed the 2035 electrification target it give an “unmistakable signal to markets” and a chance to increase both renewable and nuclear electricity.

articles.title: House majority parties back full disclosure on 2027 district allocations
articles.summary: Majority parties in the House of Representatives expressed support on Monday for the full disclosure of congressional district allocations under the proposed 2027 national budget.

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 1:37am
Majority parties in the House of Representatives expressed support on Monday for the full disclosure of congressional district allocations under the proposed 2027 national budget.

In a press conference, representatives of the National Unity Party (NUP), the Nationalist People’s Coalition (NPC), the Lakas-Christian Muslim Democrats (Lakas-CMD), the Partido Federal ng Pilipinas (PFP), and the Nacionalista Party (NP) voiced support for the move.

The groups underscored that with the full disclosure of the budget, district representatives were compelled to explain how funds are distributed in their respective areas and what specific projects will be funded.

“Ang mga distrito po ay iba-iba. Iba-iba po ang character. Iba-iba po ang lokasyon. So 'yung iba may kailangan na mga sea wall. Sa urbanized area, wala,” Camarines Sur 4th District Representative Arnie Fuentebella said.
(Districts vary in character and location. Some areas need seawalls, while urbanized areas do not.)
“So regarding this matter, wala po kaming problema na ipakita kung ano 'yung mga proyekto sa kanya-kanyang distrito,” he added.
(Regarding this matter, we have no problem disclosing the projects lined up for our respective district.)
Surigao del Sur 1st District Representative Romeo Momo Sr. doubled down on Fuentebella’s point, noting the NP’s non-objection to disclosing district allocations.

Momo pointed out that given the varying needs of each district, funding allocations naturally differ. Because of these distinct regional needs, he argued, allocations should be scrutinized to ensure every district receives sufficient funding for its programs.

“We believe that there is no equal allocation in each district, wala hong equal talaga, otherwise hindi na tayo magdi-discuss pa dito ng review ng ating budget kung pare-parehas lang naman. The distribution of the budget is on the needs of its district,” Momo said.

(We believe that there is no equal allocation for each district—there is truly no uniform amount. Otherwise, we wouldn't even be discussing a budget review here if everything were identical. The distribution of the budget is based on the needs of each district.)

“Kaya nga kanina sinabi ni Cong Abet na iba-iba ang karakteristik ng bawat distrito. May malalaking distrito, may mga distritong dinadaanan ng bagyo, may mga distrito maraming river systems, may mga distrito na laging prone to typhoon and earthquakes. So lahat po ito'y kinukonsider ng distribution ng ating budget,” he added.

(That's why Congressman Abet earlier mentioned that every district has different characteristics. There are large districts, districts hit frequently by typhoons, districts with extensive river systems, and districts prone to earthquakes. All of these factors are considered in the distribution of our budget.)

Representing Lakas-CMD and the PFP respectively, Negros Oriental 3rd District Representative Janice Degamo and Davao del Norte 2nd District Representative JM Lagdameo likewise expressed support for the full disclosure of congressional district budgets.
Degamo said all members of Lakas are open to disclosing their budgets, stressing that they have nothing to hide.
In October, the House approved on final reading its proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027 under House Bill No. 10858.
Even as the measure is already under review in the Senate, several sectors continue to raise concerns over amendments made by the House Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee (BARSc).
The People's Budget Coalition (PBC) watchdog flagged over P1 trillion in "red flags" under the House-approved 2027 budget, particularly regarding various forms of discretionary or "pork" funds.

Among those cited by the PBC are P210 billion in "soft pork" in the form of patronage-driven aid, P695 billion in "hard pork" or politicized infrastructure, and P112 billion in "shadow pork" or unprogrammed appropriations.
Through Deputy Speaker Ronaldo Puno of Antipolo, the NUP earlier announced its members' willingness to disclose the budget amendments they included in the proposed 2027 budget.
Puno said he had already taken the lead by disclosing and explaining his district's projects directly to the PBC. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Leni Robredo-Raffy Tulfo leading Baste Duterte-Robin Padilla -- OCTA 2028 tandem survey
articles.summary: Mayor Leni Robredo-Sen. Raffy Tulfo tandem leads Mayor Baste Duterte-Sen. Robin Padilla in a hypothetical 2028 presidential and vice presidential tandem matchup, according to OCTA"s First 2028 Tandem…

blocks.text: Mayor Leni Robredo–Sen. Raffy Tulfo tandem leads Mayor Baste Duterte–Sen. Robin Padilla in a hypothetical 2028 presidential and vice presidential tandem matchup, according to OCTA’s First 2028 Tandem Survey.
Nationwide, at least 43% of adult Filipinos say they would vote for the Robredo–Tulfo tandem while 39% will choose the Duterte-Padilla tandem, while 18% choose neither tandem or say they do not know.
Among the 1,170 respondents who reported being registered voters, the results are virtually the same: 43% for the Robredo–Tulfo tandem, 40% for the Duterte–Padilla tandem, and 17% uncommitted.

In OCTA’s first survey of this hypothetical 2028 pairing, the Robredo–Tulfo tandem leads nationally by four points, just above the ±3% margin of error. OCTA underscored that the figures cannot yet show whether support for either tandem is rising or falling.

The results reflect voter preferences at the time of fieldwork, from September 28 to October 4, 2026, roughly 19 months before the May 2028 elections and more than a month before Mayor Leni Robredo’s November 9 reiteration that she will not run.

With 18% of voters uncommitted and the Visayas and Class D evenly split, the results set a baseline for a contest that is still taking shape, the key findings from the third quarter Tugon ng Masa (TNM) are non-commissioned nationwide survey showed.
The survey is an independent and non-partisan poll conducted regularly by OCTA Research.

The survey fieldwork was conducted using face-to face interviews of 1,200 probability respondents aged 18 and above, both male and female, were interviewed for the study. The survey has a ±3% margin of error at a 95% confidence level.

Mayor Leni Robredo announced in April 2026 that she will not run for President in 2028, and she again reiterated this positionon November 9, 2026, describing the matter as closed, stating that she does not intend to return to national politics, and indicating that she will instead seek reelection as mayor of Naga City.

"While OCTA acknowledges Mayor Leni Robredo’s statement, it should be stressed that the survey was conducted from September 28 to October 4, 2026 — more than a month before her November 9 statement — and therefore does not reflect any public reaction to it."
Mayor Baste Duterte, for his part, has not declared a presidential bid. Neither tandem is a declared ticket.

With fieldwork conducted from September 28 to October 4, 2026, coincided with the Senate impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte are not reflected in the survey results, and OCTA draws no inference about the effect of the proceedings on voter preferences.

The OCTA Research said the results of the probe are not a forecast, and they are likely to change as the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte proceeds and as candidacies, alliances, and public issues develop.
Ethnoliguistic, geographic divide
"Beneath the national figures, the two tandems appear to draw on distinct coalitions, and the sharpest lines between them may be ethnolinguistic and geographic rather than socioeconomic."

The Robredo–Tulfo tandem leads by wide margins among Tagalog/Filipino (54% to 24%) and Ilocano (80% to 8%) respondents, while the Duterte–Padilla tandem leads 75% to 10% among Cebuano/Bisaya respondents; Ilonggo respondents are closely divided (42% to 40%).
Tagalog/Filipino speakers make up 57% of the Robredo–Tulfo tandem’s voters, while Cebuano/Bisaya speakers make up 46% of the Duterte–Padilla tandem’s voters.
Socioeconomic classes
By contrast, differences across socioeconomic classes are more modest: Class D, about four in five adults, is evenly split at 41% each.

The Robredo–Tulfo coalition appears anchored in Luzon. The tandem leads 61% to 19% in Balance Luzon, rising to 69% in North Luzon, and 49% to 32% in NCR, and about four in five of its voters (80%) live in Luzon. It also leads in Western Visayas (60%) and the Negros Island Region (62%), and among women (47% to 36%), urban residents (48% to 36%), voters aged 45 and above, Classes ABC (53% to 29%) and E (48% to 37%), and college-educated respondents (46% to 33%).

The Duterte–Padilla coalition appears anchored in Mindanao and Central Visayas. The tandem leads 81% to 4% in Mindanao, with shares of 84% to 90% in Davao Region, SOCCSKSARGEN, CARAGA and BARMM, and 79% in Central Visayas.

Nearly half of its voters (47%) live in Mindanao, but more than half live elsewhere, and NCR is its second largest regional source of voters. It leads among men (43% to 39%), rural residents (43% to 36%), voters aged 25 to 44, respondents with no formal or elementary education (47% to 37%), and the D2 segment of Class D (45% to 37%). Between these bases lies a contested middle.
The Visayas as a whole (43% Duterte-Padilla, 41% Robredo–Tulfo), Class D, voters aged 18 to 24 (39% to 38%), and high school educated respondents (43% to 41%) are closely divided.

The uncommitted bloc — 18% nationally, more than four times the gap — is concentrated in South Luzon and among younger voters, with shares of 32% in CALABARZON and 36% in rural South Luzon, and its eventual choices may pull in different directions.

"With the lead slight, the uncommitted bloc large, and the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte still unresolved, this matchup remains an early and open baseline — not a prediction of the May 2028 outcome," the group said. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: France blames Iran for cyberattack that hacked supermarket refrigerators across the country

image.caption: A view of the closed frozen food aisle at a supermarket near Nantes is shown on Oct. 12, after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains. (Stephanie Mahe/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot ‌on Monday accused Iran's ​Revolutionary Guards of being ​behind a recent cyberattack ​on French supermarket fridges, saying ‌there would be consequences for the country.
France cyberattack was followed by a more widespread European wave of attacks several days later

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot ‌on Monday accused Iran's ​Revolutionary Guards of being ​behind a recent cyberattack ​on French ⁠supermarket refrigerators, ⁠saying ‌there would be consequences for the ⁠country.

Meanwhile, the Paris prosecutor's office ‌said it had requested international arrest warrants against ​the ⁠leader of Shahid Kaveh, ⁠an offensive ⁠cyber ⁠unit ​affiliated with the Revolutionary ​Guards, ⁠and his two deputies.

The Oct. 11 cyberattack, which overrode the temperature controls on commercial fridges in hundreds of establishments, appeared to have been easy to pull off, cybersecurity experts previously ​told Reuters. The firm behind many of the stricken units said that several were obsolete or were ⁠running outdated firmware, which could have made ⁠it easy for hackers to break in.

The effects were still dramatic. ‌Some refrigerators had the temperature turned up so high they caught fire. In the hours following the hack, supermarket employees carted boxes full of perished meat and melted ice cream into giant trash containers.
Hackers target European supermarket fridges, millions in spoiled food tossed
The attack's total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros countrywide, one French supermarket owner estimated.

The hacks were followed this month by a second wave of hacking that hit more than 100 establishments across Europe and even affected refrigerators used by French blood banks, prompting employees there to have to ‌move some of the blood to different cold storage units.

The seemingly straightforward nature of the refrigerator hacks — and their repetition across multiple countries — prompted speculation about who might be responsible amid ongoing concerns over Russia's suspected sabotage campaign in Europe, the war between the U.S. and Iran and the global rise of AI-powered cyberattacks.
The sabotage of European supermarket ​fridges was preceded by at least one similar incident in the United States.

In August, refrigerators in at least half a dozen military commissaries went out of commission. Pentagon investigators ⁠are treating the malfunctions as a suspected cyberattack and are working with French officials to get to the bottom of what happened, Reuters ⁠reported last month.

blocks.text: Reuters could not independently establish whether there was any link between the refrigeration incidents at U.S. military bases in ⁠August, the ⁠hacking campaign in France and the more recent ​wave of refrigeration hacks that struck Europe.

The Pentagon said on Monday that it is "aware of speculation regarding a potential cyber incident" but that military investigators were on the case and it could not offer further comment ⁠for security reasons.

articles.title: Only known handwritten final draft of MLK Jr’s I Have A Dream speech to be auctioned
articles.summary:
The document is expected to fetch more than $10m and the proceeds will be donated to several charities

The likely only surviving handwritten final full draft of Martin Luther King Jr’s…

blocks.text: The likely only surviving handwritten final full draft of Martin Luther King Jr’s historic 1963 I Have a Dream speech is set to be auctioned in New York City in January, with proceeds benefiting several charities, including the King Center in Atlanta, Georgia.

Auction house Christie’s has announced that the document is expected to fetch more than $10m, and that the pages will be displayed publicly at the auction house from 15 to 21 January, before being offered in a single-lot sale.

Described as “the only known handwritten final draft of the speech”, the auction house said that the document was rediscovered in 2024 in a desk drawer belonging to a former aide of King’s, Edward T Clayton, by his widow, Xernona.

She had originally found it in the late 1990s but did not know then that it was the only known final draft, and put it back in the drawer, until 2024, when she rediscovered the document and experts established that it is unique, Christie’s added.
According to the auction house, King completed the draft of the speech in the early hours of 28 August 1963, at the Willard hotel in Washington DC.

“Focused on limiting his remarks to five minutes, and considering both word choice and flow, Dr King wrote the final draft of the speech in blue ink across seven yellow legal pad pages after days of discussions with many advisers – including trusted speech writer Edward T Clayton,” Christie’s said.
Just hours after the ink dried that day, King delivered the pivotal speech in Washington DC with his towering rhetoric during the height of the civil rights struggle for racial equality in the US.

“The stirring words that he delivered that afternoon have come to be regarded as the most important speech of the 20th Century, and one of the most important speeches in American history,” the release said.
Christie’s said the pages contain edits and crossings-out and “offer a rare glimpse at Dr King’s writing process”.

Notably, this original draft does not include the words “I have a dream”, as King “famously added” those words “spontaneously while delivering his speech on the day of the [civil rights] march”, Christie’s said.

“This is a treasure of American history,” said Peter Klarnet, Christie’s manuscripts specialist. “It gives you chills to look at it. Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time. It captures a moment that literally changed the course of our nation and makes it very real and very human.”
King’s son, Martin Luther King III, said in a statement that it is “poetic that the past will protect the future”.

articles.title: France blames Iran’s Revolutionary Guards for cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges
articles.summary: French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month

blocks.text: France has said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind “unprecedented” cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in the country last month, vowing European sanctions against Tehran.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” the French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said on Monday of the hacks on 11 and 12 October.
“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” he said, adding, “We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack.”
Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations.

The October hacks were followed this month by a second wave of hacking ‌that hit more than 100 establishments across Europe and even affected refrigerators used by French blood banks, prompting employees to move some of the blood to other cold storage units.

The seemingly straightforward nature of the refrigerator hacks – and their repetition ​across multiple countries – prompted speculation about who might be responsible amid ongoing concerns over Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign in Europe, the war between the US and Iran and the global rise of AI-powered cyberattacks.
after newsletter promotion
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Labour’s Brexit red lines ready for ‘dignified retirement’, says their co-author
articles.summary:
Exclusive: MP Chris Ward believes ditching pledges and forming closer ties with EU would protect it from global threats

One of the architects of Keir Stamer’s Brexit red lines has called for…

blocks.text: One of the architects of Keir Stamer’s Brexit red lines has called for Andy Burnham to abandon them at the next election, saying a new relationship with the EU would protect the UK from global threats.

The call is the latest voice from a prominent figure in Starmer’s administration for a faster transition to a far closer European relationship, after the former chancellor Rachel Reeves said it was right for Burnham to consider rejoining.
Chris Ward, one of Starmer’s closest confidants in politics and one of the ministers who worked on the EU reset, said that it was the security relationship that meant a change was now imperative.

The Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven said it was now time to give a “a dignified retirement” to the red lines, which rule out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union and restoring freedom of movement.
Ward also suggested there was little compelling argument for rejoining the single market without full EU membership, saying he had “never understood the argument for the latter without the former”.

But he said the main reason for abandoning the red lines was that the UK “could no longer rely on the Americans” which was a major geopolitical shift that merited an entire reappraisal of Britain’s diplomatic relationships. “That question was unthinkable in 2016, but it is unavoidable in 2026,” he wrote in an article for the Guardian.

Ward, who was Starmer’s chief adviser as shadow Brexit secretary and who co-authored the red lines in Labour’s manifesto in 2024, said that they had now outlived their usefulness and should no longer be part of Labour’s future thinking.
He remains close to the former prime minister and said that the drive to renew the relationship with the EU may prove the defining political moment of this autumn.
He said the party had agreed upon the red lines in the manifesto because they were “designed precisely to close down the debate and to narrow the target that Brexit had become for Labour”.

“I still believe that strategically this was the right course for Labour, and the reset deal that – touch wood – will get over the line at next month’s UK-EU summit will demonstrate that real benefits can be delivered within those red lines, whether cheaper prices for businesses, a youth mobility scheme or the return of the Erasmus+ scheme.

“By the next general election, however, those red lines will have served their purpose. They should be given a well-earned and dignified retirement. Frankly, they no longer speak to the world as it is in 2026, let alone as it may be over the years to come.”
Ward said it was well known that rejoining the EU or single market would have economic benefits but said supporters of rejoining should make a different argument.
“Pinning the case for a new relationship on old arguments risks both the same result and missing what’s really changed,” he wrote.

“Instead, its the huge geopolitical shifts and, above all, the new security and cyber threats the UK and Europe now face day in, day out that demand we now reassess the depth and nature of relationship.”
after newsletter promotion
He said Starmer had twice had to scramble alliances together – on Ukraine and on the strait of Hormuz – because “we could no longer rely on the Americans”.

“It would now be brave in the extreme to continue to pin our future security – and that of Europe – on the outcome of US elections, or the false hope that whoever is in the White House we can still bank on the US as we did in 2016, let alone 1945.”
Ward said there should be public debate on whether the UK should formally rejoin or seek a form of associate membership like Canada.

But he said the prime minister will “need to be clear as to why now is the right time to reopen the Brexit debate, what we are seeking, and why it is so important to our national interest. A re-run of the tired arguments of 2016 won’t do that. Defending red lines designed for 2020 won’t do that either. But appreciating the urgent strategic challenges of the decades to come just might.”
Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday, expected to be used to see Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.

Burnham will also meet European leaders on the sidelines to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to seek a closer and more permanent relationship – including potentially rejoining the bloc.
At a Brexit reset meeting on 20 November in Brussels, the UK will sign new agreements on agriculture and food, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

The prime minister is then expected to give a speech after the summit on options for the future relationship. Burnham has said previously an option to rejoin the single market could be offered in a Labour manifesto but fully rejoining would need a referendum.

articles.title: Men recruited to French gang as children to kill give rare insight into drug underworld
articles.summary: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members spoke to the BBC.

blocks.text: A BBC investigation has found one of Europe's most powerful drug gangs in France is recruiting teenage children from across the country to commit kidnap and murder.
Known as the "DZ Mafia", the gang won a bloody turf war against a rival group in Marseille during 2023, and is now recruiting from further afield.
One member who is in prison awaiting trial after being implicated in several murders told the BBC he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad.
He agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
When challenged over whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality, he says he feels "guilty in-part" but claims to have no regrets.
Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".
The BBC's Paris Correspondent, James Waterhouse, reports from Marseille.

articles.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.summary: The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up.

blocks.text: France has accused Iran of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers.
Speaking at a news conference, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of Iran.

He said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding that the country would "implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."
The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across seven other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.

Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
