articles.title: B.C. businesses push back against 'AI slop' with pen-and-paper ads
articles.summary: A marketing professor says customers are gravitating towards authenticity, as artificial intelligence is making producing perfect graphics too easy.

image.caption: Kevin Thach is the owner of NaMì Vietnamese café in Vancouver. Social media posts featuring hand-drawn depictions of his food have caused a stir online, with one expert saying customers want authenticity. (CBC News, NaMì)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A marketing professor says customers are gravitating towards authenticity, as artificial intelligence is making producing perfect graphics too easy.
Prof. says customers increasingly want authenticity as artificial intelligence makes perfection easy
They may look like they were drawn hastily by someone in a brainstorming meeting, but recent advertisements from the Vietnamese café NaMì in downtown Vancouver caused a stir online.
The ads feature extremely basic renditions of the café's banh mi sandwich and a frozen coffee drink, drawn with a black marker, along with two sheets of paper with text.
"We will NOT use AI to promote our business ... we're going old school and using a Sharpie and paper!" read the sheets of paper.
NaMì's frozen coffee advertisement is drawn in the same style as that of the banh mi sandwich. The Facebook post accompanying the ads have garnered thousands of views. (NaMì/Facebook)

As restaurants around the world turn to artificial intelligence (AI) images to save costs amid razor-thin margins, NaMì owner Kevin Thach said the pen-and-paper advertising is a way of differentiating his business.

"As we get into kind of more of an era where like you see less and less people interact with people, you kind of want to remind yourself that you're not just buying food," Thach said of his pen-and-paper strategy.
"Someone had to make that food behind ... the counter. And, you know, there's effort that gets put into it as well," he added.
AI food pics on menus leave some customers with a bad taste
The rise of AI-generated restaurant images in particular have prompted blowback online, with businesses accused of peddling "AI slop."
Thach said he thought it was bizarre that restaurants would depict their own food with perfectly-manicured or erroneous AI images.
"How can you let that be displayed as your own food? ... I never find it all too appealing or appetizing," he said.
Customers embracing authenticity
A marketing professor says customers are gravitating towards authenticity, especially from local businesses that they want to know and connect with.

"When everybody can create a perfect piece of content, when imperfection is effectively non-existent, something that is imperfect or human starts to stand out from the crowd," said Jarrett Vaughan, an adjunct professor at the University of British Columbia's business school.

items: AI 'slop' is dominating menus, as some restaurant owners turn to it to save time and money

blocks.text: Vaughan said small businesses don't need to outspend big companies in order to advertise effectively — but rather, they need to "out-humanize" them and create relationships with customers.
He acknowledged, however, that not everyone may be taken in by the AI pushback or the pen-and-paper ads.
The professor said creating a large volume of content efficiently can be difficult for small businesses, especially if resources are limited.
What do you think of restaurants using AI 'slop'?
"Obviously, we need to understand our goals and objectives and who is our target segment. We don't just create AI slop," he said.
"We do want to make sure it's authentic to the brand, but it does give an opportunity to create more content."
Graphic designers feeling devalued
It isn't just restaurants that are turning to pen-and-paper advertising — a No Frills supermarket in Burnaby also saw its employees advertising weekly deals using Sharpie-drawn sheets of paper.
A No Frills supermarket in Burnaby, B.C., also turned to pen-and-paper ads to draw attention to its weekly deals last month. (No Frills (Justin’s, Burnaby Heights)/Facebook)
Meghan D'Mello, the president of the Association of Registered Graphic Designers, said advertising is traditionally the bulk of work being done by professional graphics designers.

She said job descriptions for graphic designers were increasingly not focusing on design, but rather "prompting" to use for AI image-generating services, and some of the profession's skills were being devalued.

"There's a lot of anything that designers can do people claim can be generated by AI — which is unfortunate, because AI can never replace ... the attention to detail that professional designers have been trained to work with," she said.

items: Graphic design students say they're waiting out wave of AI advertising

blocks.text: D'Mello said she hoped customers would show businesses how they felt about using AI-generated images by voting with their wallets and not patronizing them.
She acknowledged that AI can be used to streamline working processes, but said it isn't the same as the creativity or ingenuity that designers have.
"Just remember to use your own brains and your talents and what makes you special. And that's how your customers and clients will respond," she advised fellow designers.

articles.title: Inuvik killed dozens of grizzly bears at a dump this summer. Experts say it may have been the kindest option
articles.summary: This summer, over 28 grizzly bears were shot in Inuvik. While some people are now wondering why the Department of Environment has to ‘dispatch’ problem bears, instead of relocating them or leaving…

image.caption: Grizzly bears have been visiting the Inuvik dump literally for generations, like this one pictured in 2017. But when their numbers soared, the dump was fenced this summer. (Steven Baryluk/GNWT)

blocks.text: Canada

This summer, over 28 grizzly bears were shot in Inuvik. While some people are now wondering why the Department of Environment has to ‘dispatch’ problem bears, instead of relocating them or leaving them alone, experts say death may be the kindest option.
40 bears were using the landfill as a food source. After the town fenced it off, most of them were killed
Inuvik has a bear problem. And experts say the only viable solution may be deadly.

In 2025, researchers from the N.W.T. Department of Environment and Climate Change captured 3,936 bear detections on trail cameras, with up to 13 bears in a frame at one time. DNA analysis found upwards of 40 bears were regularly using the dump as a dining room.
Since the town erected an electric fence around the landfill, as first reported by Cabin Radio, most of the bears haven’t made it.

Estimates vary, but Toby Halle, a renewable resource officer based in Inuvik, says at least 28 of them were shot by officers, with more shot by locals. The chance of the remaining few surviving is slim, he said.
“Their fate was pretty much written in the stars, I guess,” said Halle.
In 2025, researchers could spot multiple bears in one frame from trail cameras, sometimes as many as 13. (Government of the Northwest Territories)

Under orders from the Gwich'in Land and Water Board, officials built an electric fence around the dump to keep the bears out. It's a model being used by other dumps across North America, but so far, Inuvik is the only community in the Beaufort Delta region to do so.
It cost the town close to a million dollars, paid for in part by federal funds, says Inuvik Mayor Peter Clarkson.
“There was lots of anxiety in town for sure. And lots of people questioning why was the town doing this? Isn't it better to just let the bears feed at the landfill in the long term?" Clarkson said.
“No, it's not better because this is the situation you get.”
The electricity was turned on this summer. But the problem didn’t go away. Instead, bears started descending on Inuvik in search of food.
Others were spotted prowling the fence in desperation.
One of the grizzly bears captured by trail cameras prowling the Inuvik dump in May, 2026. (Government of the Northwest Territories)

“They would just do these laps around the dump and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Halle. “They don't know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don't know what to do with them.”
The problem is that for many of these bears, the dump was all they’d ever known.

“We've probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said Clarkson, based on the math that female grizzlies can start having cubs around age 7. “Unfortunately, something wasn't done 25 years ago.”
After the electric fence was switched on in April, many bears "didn't know what to do with themselves," say Toby Halle, renewable resource officer. (Government of the Northwest Territories)
Clarkson says thankfully there were no tragic bear encounters, but people in Inuvik spent the summer on high alert.
“We'd be inundated with bear calls,” said Halle.
He says in the past the department tried to relocate one family group, but they returned within days.

Dr. Lana Ciarniello is an independent conservation scientist and co-chair of the human-bear conflicts expert team with the International Union for Conservation of Nature. She says moving bears elsewhere, especially in the N.W.T. — where there are healthy bear populations everywhere — is not a viable solution.
“Where are you going to move them? You're going to move them into someone else's home,” she said, adding this increases the odds of one bear killing another.
“Moving bears is not the solution.”

In Europe, where she says there are no-kill policies, some problematic bears have been put into captivity. But she says many of these wild bears are not adapting well to captivity, and Canada doesn't have enough specialized facilities to take them in.
The solution, therefore, is prevention.
"Bears cannot be feeding on garbage. It is 2026. I mean, it's ridiculous to have open pit dumps anywhere in Canada. They need to be closed," she said.
Many bears had grown up relying on the Inuvik landfill as a food source, like this one pictured in 2017. (Steven Baryluk/Government of the Northwest Territories)
Halle says the next couple of years will see slightly higher bear activity, before it normalizes.
That is, as long as the fence stays up — and the town makes sure it’s bear proof.
“We make these bears,” said Ciarniello. “They're not problems inherently on their own."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jessica Davey-Quantick has been reporting in the North since 2016. She holds a Bachelor of Journalism (Honours) from the University of King's College, and a Master of Arts in Cultural Studies from Queen's University for her thesis, Dumpcano: Waste Management and Environmental Justice in Iqaluit. You can reach her at jessica.davey-quantick@cbc.ca.

articles.title: EU aims to pick new ECB chief by year-end
articles.summary: Christine Lagarde's early decision to step down as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) has put the European Union on a tight schedule. The bloc expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of…

image.caption: The successors for the ECB's top jobs would likely be negotiated among the main eurozone countriesImage: KIRILL KUDRYAVTSEV/AFP

blocks.text: The European Union (EU) wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday.
Christine Lagarde, who has headed the ECB for seven years, has announced on October 29 that she is stepping down prematurely from the position, nine months ⁠before ⁠the end of her term.
Lagarde's early decision to step down makes the schedule tight because leaders must also fill two other seats on the ECB's Executive Board ​within months.
"The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year," Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of eurozone finance ministers.
Who pays for Europe’s economic independence?

"We understand that we need to move fast. But what has traditionally happened in ​the past is that this was a decision driven by the leaders. Today it will be primarily an information point and the discussion," he said.
Who are the candidates?
The two candidates to replace Lagarde are former Dutch Central Bank Governor Klaas Knot and the head of the Bank for International ​Settlements, Pablo ‌Hernandez de Cos from Spain.

Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU governments' heads.
The appointment process requires eurozone finance ministers to put forward a candidate, followed by a European Parliament hearing and a final decision by EU leaders.
Dutch minister says the choice needs to be 'merit based'
Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the "right person for the position", referring to his long-standing experience.
"He knows the ECB inside out. He's been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus," he told reporters.
EU wants to attract European savers to boost bloc's economy

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, on the other hand, said Knot was an "excellent candidate", adding: "He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfil this position."

Heinen also ​said countries should ‌not see the ECB leadership contest as ​one between northern ⁠and southern European countries, or as ⁠an "​opportunity to trade favors" on other topics such as the multi-year EU budget.
A package deal is expected

The other two seats which have to be filled are those of Isabel ‌Schnabel, the head of the ECB's market operations, who leaves on January 3, 2027, and Chief Economist Philip Lane, ​whose term ends ⁠in May 2027.
The three jobs are likely to be negotiated between the ⁠main eurozone countries — ​France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands — as a package, Reuters news agency said, citing officials.
The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three positions.
Can Europe's economy survive in a new world order?
"Perhaps this would facilitate things. But again, this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders at the leaders level," Pierrakakis said.
Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde's replacement would be chosen by December.
"It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible," he said. But it's also about getting it right and getting the right person. It's a really crucial appointment."

items: Twenty senators have urged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity due to the impacts of Super El Niño, which would allow access to necessary funds.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CEBU, Philippines – Twenty senators on Monday, November 9, have called on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in areas affected or threatened by the Super El Niño, allowing access to funds to combat the weather phenomenon’s impact on the country.

Under Republic Act No. 10121, the declaration of a state of calamity mandates remedial measures such as the imposition of a price ceiling on basic necessities and commodities, monitoring and prevention of hoarding and profiteering activities, programming of funds for the repair and upgrading of public infrastructure, and the granting of no-interest loans to affected communities.

Upon the recommendation of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), the senators, through Proposed Senate Resolution No. 765, urged the President to declare a state of calamity to address challenges being faced primarily by the agricultural sector.

Among those who signed the resolution were Senate President Win Gatchalian, Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto, and senators Kiko Pangilinan, Migz Zubiri, Bam Aquino, Risa Hontiveros, JV Ejercito, Lito Lapid, Joel Villanueva, Erwin Tulfo, Raffy Tulfo, Ping Lacson, Chiz Escudero, Alan Peter Cayetano, Pia Cayetano, Imee Marcos, Robin Padilla, Bong Go, Camille Villar, and Mark Villar.

According to the Department of Agriculture, the country has reported P6.87 billion in agricultural losses across 249,028 hectares as of September 26 — nearly half of the recorded losses during the 2023-2024 El Niño.

“Planting season ngayon sa ating mga palayan at kailangan ng tubig. Kailangan mag-plant din tayo ng mga remedial measure tulad ng pag-impose ng price ceilings at laban sa overpricing, profiteering, at hoarding,” Pangilinan said.
(It’s planting season in our rice fields, and we need water. We also need to plant remedial measures, such as imposing price ceilings and policies against overpricing, profiteering, and hoarding)

On November 5, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) announced that a very strong El Niño was present in the tropical Pacific Ocean and is expected to persist until the first half of 2027.

According to PAGASA, the weather phenomenon will potentially reach its peak by the end of 2026, increasing the likelihood of rainfall deficits and, consequently, raising the odds of dry spells and drought in the country.

“Based on the latest drought assessment, five provinces experienced meteorological drought, 11 provinces were under dry spell, and 10 provinces experienced dry conditions in October 2026,” PAGASA Administrator Nathaniel Servando said in a statement.

The Senate resolution stated that while more than a hundred cities and municipalities have declared a state of calamity, the Department of Agriculture has managed to provide aid to only 2.53 million out of 11.12 million target beneficiaries. This means only one in five farmers are getting the help they need amid drought and dry conditions.
According to the senators, around P39 billion is available under the country’s disaster response fund. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Drug possession is illegal. Why can people use openly in public?

image.caption: The number of reports of discarded needles and open drug use to the City of St. John's 311 hotline have increased in the last several years. (CBC News Graphics)

blocks.text: A man reaches with a pair of tongs underneath a large rock and grabs a bundle of needles, dropping them into a yellow disposal bin.
"This may be a record," he says.
It's a Monday morning in October and staff at a St. John's community centre are doing their daily sweeps, to keep used needles out of areas used by children.

"In the last three years we definitely had an extreme uprise [of] even more of the drug paraphernalia being seen around the area," said Enid Pendergast, executive director of the Froude Avenue Community Centre.

If you haven’t seen it yourself, like Pendergast, you’ve likely seen it online. Social media is awash with photos and comments about open drug use and discarded needles littering public parks and benches, prompting questions about public drug consumption and the law.

There are a skyrocketing number of reports citing discarded needles and open drug use to the capital city's hotline, 311. Records obtained through access-to-information show there were over 1,000 calls to the city about needles and open consumption over the last two years. That's a dramatic increase from 2016, when there were 181 such reports.

But data from Statistics Canada shows federal prosecutors are handling fewer simple drug possession cases across the country than ever before. In Newfoundland and Labrador, there has been an overall 10-year decline.

The drop in prosecutions — and the apparent rise in open usage — coincides with a Public Prosecution Service of Canada policy change in 2020 directing prosecutors away from laying criminal charges for drug possession, according to police officials and experts who spoke with CBC News.
A staff member of the Froude Avenue Community Centre picks up a bundle of used needles one Monday morning in October. (Ted Dillon/CBC)
The Froude Avenue Community Centre is centrally located in St. John's, and has paths coming to and from main thoroughfares like Blackmarsh and Mundy Pond roads and Campbell Avenue.

"Maybe we're like a hideaway spot or a comfortable spot ... where people come to do whatever it is that they need to do and the stuff just kind of gets left behind," Pendergast said in a recent interview.

An increase in public consumption and discarded needles has changed the way the centre runs their operations and allows children in their care to play. A couple of winters ago, kids in afterschool programs were unable to play in the snow over concerns of needles hiding underneath.

They've had to fence in their backyard to avoid open drug use on their premises, and children are no longer allowed to walk back and forth alone from nearby schools. That decision was made two years ago, when children came to Pendergast with a concern.
Enid Pendergast is the executive director of the Froude Avenue Community Centre. (Ted Dillon/CBC)
"The children said, 'Hey Miss, we just saw someone and they were in the pathway,' and they knew that they were using," she recalled.

Having spent decades working at the centre, Pendergast says she's also noticed another change. Attitudes of those openly using have shifted in recent years — a development that has made her more cautious in her approach.

"Before, in the past years, [it was] always so much easier in going talking to people, I believe because they didn't want children to see what they were doing, honestly. Before, if you had to speak to them, they would gladly put something away," she said.
"Over the last year, I would not go out and ask anybody now to move or put those things away because the response back just isn't the same."
And Pendergast says it's not a problem solely in her area. She has run into issues on field trips with the children in parks around the city.

Pendergast says it's a tough balance — keeping kids safe, while understanding the problems are complex. She says she doesn't judge, knows that addiction is a disease, and believes the support isn't sufficient for those who want it.
Why open drug use may not result in criminal charges
Criminal sanctions have 'limited effectiveness'
The law also views substance use as a health issue — not a criminal one. The principle is rooted in updated guidelines in 2020 by the Public Prosecution Service of Canada.
It advises prosecutors to prioritize health alternatives and diversion over criminal charges.
They reserve that for cases that pose serious risks to public safety.

"Criminal sanctions, as a primary response, have a limited effectiveness as specific or general deterrents and as a means of addressing the public safety concerns when considering the harmful effects of criminal records and short periods of incarceration," reads a section from the PPSC guidelines.
It's not outright decriminalization, as has been piloted and ditched in British Columbia, but provides a higher threshold for prosecution.
Victoria Police Chief Constable Fiona Wilson co-chairs the drug advisory committee of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police. (Kathryn Marlow/CBC)
The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police agrees — substance use is a health issue. But without providing alternatives to criminal charges, they say police are left with few options.
The association walked back its support of B.C.'s decriminalization pilot project years after it began, because it said the policy lacked adequate guardrails around public consumption.
Victoria Police Chief Constable Fiona Wilson, who also co-chairs the association's drug advisory committee, says the PPSC guidelines present a challenge for police.
“We don't want to introduce people to the criminal justice system simply by virtue of a substance use disorder," Wilson told CBC News.
"I also feel really strongly, and I think police leadership across this country feels strongly, that our public spaces ought to be accessible and safe and usable by all members in our community.”

Wilson says part of the problem is that there are a "significant lack of alternatives," aside from bringing someone to a supervised injection site. And drug courts are only useful once someone has entered the criminal justice system.

"I've really come to this place where — although I am really apprehensive to dial back the clock in terms of arresting people and introducing them to the criminal justice system for simple possession — I deeply wish that there was an alternative for our police officers," she said.

Royal Newfoundland Constabulary Insp. Ryan Pittman says the police force's stance on public drug use is that it is a criminal offence, but notes that laying charges is not a straightforward decision. (Ted Dillon/CBC)
Back in St. John's, Royal Newfoundland Constabulary Insp. Ryan Pittman says the RNC's stance is that drug possession is an offence and will be treated as such.
However, having the proper evidence to take a case to court isn't as straightforward.

“When we're dealing with these situations we actually have to see the person consume a drug or be in possession of a drug," Pittman said. "That's hard to do and justify without a statement, or from someone who wants to be anonymous."
Pittman says all cases are different, and officers are left balancing enforcement and public health.

"Our number one priority is public safety. These open use areas are in public areas that the public — rightfully so — want to feel free and safe when they go to these. And if we can see someone using open drugs or open anything in the public area, it's our job to deal with that."

Dealing with it doesn't necessarily mean criminal charges, Pittman says. As an example, if there are children in the area, officers would make an arrest and seize any drugs, then use discretion on whether to lay charges based on legal criteria.
The force has heard loud and clear that there are concerns over open drug use — though Pittman stops short of saying there is an increase without the numbers to back it up.
“It's our job to listen to what the community wants and to prioritize and strategically align our resources with those issues," Pittman said. "And we've been doing that."
He points to increased patrols, covert surveillance, and using the mobile crisis unit in the area around the Gathering Place.

There are safe disposal boxes located around the city where individuals can discard of used needles. However, there continue to be concerns surrounding needles littering public areas. (Ted Dillon/CBC)
The shelter has become a focal point for those criticizing the lack of action on open drug use.
In response, the non-profit organization and City of St. John's announced a pilot project that pays guests for cleaning up needles and litter.

items: Gathering Place users will pick up litter, needles as part of new pilot project in St. John's

blocks.text: Gathering Place executive director Colin McNeil says he doesn’t condone open drug use but if someone is homeless, they may have few other options.
McNeil — a former deputy chief of the RNC — doesn't believe charging them is appropriate.

“Really and truly, what are we trying to address here? It’s a catch and release game … someone gets arrested, they go to court, they’re out the next day doing the same thing," McNeil said in a recent interview with CBC News.
"So, what have we done? We just clogged up our justice system with a health-related issue.”
McNeil knows the complications of policing drug cases first hand, and believes people have to be held accountable for using openly — but how?
"We need to come up with better options. And what are they? I haven't figured that out yet. Neither has the rest of the country."

articles.title: Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global…

image.caption: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993Image: Joyce N. Boghosian/White House/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.
The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believes she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.
US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.
What has Nvidia and the US government said?

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.
Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

blocks.caption: Nvidia chips are used to build and run AI applications Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."
The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.
While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.
"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."
Why it matters for Nvidia

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.
"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

blocks.caption: The sale of Nvidia chips to China is a major political sorepointImage: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, says the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Jensen Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.
"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."
The tangled China-Nvidia web
Nvidia and Huang's attitude towards China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed their sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-licence review. Beijing has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.
Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

blocks.caption: Nvidia is at the center of the US-China rivalry in AI Image: Huang Jingwen/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials, who fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost their domestic AI sector, lead to their AI models catching up with the leading US models and could be used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.
What China hopes to gain
Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Richard Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also casts doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.
"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

blocks.caption: While China has made advances it AI, it lacks advanced chips Image: Jung Yeon-je/AFP

blocks.text: The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom, thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.
Its valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.
Edited by Nik Martin

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

articles.title: Deportation policy ‘might have been too tough’, says Trump, as Miller starts chief-of-staff role – US politics live
articles.summary: President’s admission appears at odds with the elevation of immigration hardliner

blocks.text: Key events

items: 36m agoTrump says deportation policy 'might have been too tough' ahead of Miller's first day as chief of staff

blocks.caption: Robert Mackey

blocks.text: Robert Mackey

Donald Trump said on Sunday that he “was only kidding” when he announced a day earlier that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

Speaking to reporters on his way back the White House from his beach club in Florida, Trump explained the premise of his joke, that if the UFC boss, who is a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room, flanked by six fighters, reporters “wouldn’t mess around with him so much”.

“So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump added. “Of course, I was kidding. And you could see that because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all going to come with him … It was just a little fun.”

Earlier on Sunday, the president shared an animated AI cartoon made by one of his supporters on social media, which showed UFC fighters beating up journalists and one, Josh Hokit, repeating the racist remark about Michelle Obama he made during the UFC event at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June.

The president said that his mock announcement that White would become his spokesperson, in a social media post on Saturday, “was an example of something where I was kidding, and then people said, ‘You know, that’s actually a pretty good idea’”.

blocks.caption: Adam Gabbatt

blocks.text: Adam Gabbatt

Stephen Miller, the influential architect of Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, is due to start as White House chief of staff today. His promotion has horrified many, handing even more power to the president’s most controversial aide.

The 41-year-old has been with Trump since the beginning of the US president’s political career – serving as a speechwriter during his 2016 presidential campaign – and has long been seen as a hardliner on the right, serving as the driving force behind first-term Trump policies such as family separation at the US-Mexico border and the travel ban on people from many Muslim-majority countries.
Here is Miller in some of his own words:
Trump says deportation policy 'might have been too tough' ahead of Miller's first day as chief of staff
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.
The president said, in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, that his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost.
He told CBS’s ‘60 Minutes’ in an interview that aired on Sunday:
double quotation markI think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.

The president’s comments were an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.
Trump said that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority, adding:
double quotation markWe would work something out. And I think it’s something - I think that’s something that’s actually doable.

The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

His comments come as his most controversial aide Miller was due today to start his new role as chief of staff. In a social media ‌post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of ​my most trusted advisors” and praised the outgoing Susie Wiles for doing “an ⁠outstanding job”.
Read our full report here:
In other developments:

items: On the race among Republicans to succeed him for the 2028 presidential election, Trump hinted at staying neutral. Asked whether he’d endorse a potential successor, the president said “probably, not necessarily.” “We have a tremendous bench. I have so many people that I have great relationships with,” Trump said in his CBS interview.

Trump said on Sunday that he “was only kidding” when he announced a day earlier that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC). Speaking to reporters on his way back the White House from his beach club in Florida, Trump explained the premise of his joke, that if the UFC boss, who is a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room, flanked by six fighters, reporters “wouldn’t mess around with him so much”.

Trump will meet with Qatar’s prime minister at ⁠the White House today, according to the White House schedule, as the ⁠conflict with ⁠Iran ​drags on and diplomatic efforts to end it face significant obstacles. Trump is due ⁠to meet with Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who also serves as Qatar’s foreign ⁠minister, in a closed-door meeting. Vice-president JD Vance ​is also scheduled to meet ‌with the ‌Qatari leader, according to a US official.

A US deportation flight of Iranian nationals bound for Iran by way of Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, according to an attorney who spoke to some of the detainees slated for repatriation. At least eight Iranians were loaded onto a plane Sunday morning in Mesa, Arizona, for a deportation flight headed to the country of Georgia, then on to Pakistan, according to Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions on behalf of some of the Iranian detainees. The flight was canceled without explanation, he said.

articles.title: Who is Ilse Aigner, leading candidate for Germany's next president?
articles.summary: She would be the first female president and the first Christian Social Union politician to hold Germany's highest office. Ilse Aigner is the favored candidate for the Federal Convention vote on…

image.caption: Ilse Aigner is likely to be Germany's next presidentImage: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner has emerged as the leading candidate to succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as president of Germany, a largely ceremonial figure who is nevertheless the official head of state, and regarded as a moral authority for the nation.

German chancellor and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) leader Friedrich Merz announced over the weekend that he favored Aigner, a veteran of the CDU's sister-party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and currently president of the Bavarian parliament.

A specially convened assembly, the Federal Convention, will gather on January 30, 2027, to elect the next German president, and since the CDU, CSU, and their coalition partner the Social Democratic Party (SPD) have a majority in the convention, Aigner's election is considered highly likely.
Could Ilse Aigner become Germany's first female head of state?
An electrician who knows how to network

Ilse Aigner is in many respects an unusual politician, especially in Germany: She has no university degree, though, as the youngest of four sisters, she did train as a telecommunications technician to join her parent's electricians' company.
She spent several years working for the military helicopter company Eurocopter, since bought by the aviation and defense giant Airbus, where she developed electrical components.

She entered the Bavarian parliament for the CSU in 1994. From 1998 to 2013 she served in Germany's federal parliament, the Bundestag, for the last six years of which she was agriculture and consumer protection minister under CDU Chancellor Angela Merkel. Both these portfolios involved holding off considerable pressure from the public and powerful lobbying organizations, as well as conflicts in the EU. Aigner came through this period without major crises and was highly esteemed in government.

The personnel policies of political parties can often seem like a game of chess. In 2013, Aigner left national politics and moved back to her home state to serve as Bavaria's economy minister under then State Premier Horst Seehofer, who tried to establish her as his successor.
Colleagues and competitors: Söder and Aigner

But then came Markus Söder, then Bavarian finance minister and for a long time Seehofer's biggest rival inside the CSU. It was Söder, a colorful character who also harbored pretensions to be German chancellor, who won out in the power struggle that followed Seehofer's retirement and became Bavarian state premier in 2018.

Aigner and Söder both entered Bavaria's state parliament in 1994, when they were the state's two youngest lawmakers, and their political paths have been intertwined since. Though Söder's rise to power prevented Aigner from becoming state premier, she has served as president of Bavaria's state parliament for the past eight years, and is a highly respected authority figure in the state.
For months now, Aigner has been named as a potential candidate for Germany's head of state after Steinmeier's constitutionally-enforced exit next year.

Söder himself openly mentioned her as a suitable candidate back in April, and there have been indications of support from several CDU and CSU representatives, but also from the ranks of the center-left SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But Merz seemed wary for a long time. Other names came – and went.

When the chancellor greeted Aigner by name in his opening remarks to a CSU meeting in Munich in October, he had to pause for thunderous applause from the delegates, who rose to their feet to celebrate the veteran politician.

In January, the Bavarian Merkur newspaper reported on Aigner's visit to a school in the town of Tegernsee, where she answered questions from fourth graders for their student newspaper. The CSU politician told them that she had not planned her career, but she was never able to "keep her mouth shut" and this was also part of why she had been elected to her various offices.

However, it was also noticeable that she was entirely capable of "keeping her mouth shut" when it was judicious to do so: She has largely refrained from commenting publicly during the internal maneuvering for the candidacy within the Union parties.

Aigner would not only be Germany's first female president, but also the first to be single and never married. Though men have dominated the office, there have been female nominees in almost every election since 1999. In that year, the Union put forward Thuringian physicist Dagmar Schipanski, while the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), precursor to the socialist Left Party, put forward theologian Uta Ranke-Heinemann in the race against Social Democrat Johannes Rau.

But considering the majority needed in the Federal Convention, both were effectively just token candidates from minority parties, as were all the other female candidates since. That is one reason why there has been pressure to finally choose a woman as the majority candidate. Aigner has long enjoyed respect from the conservative camp.

blocks.caption: Markus Söder (as Elvis) and Ilse Aigner (as the goddess Nike) were once rivals for the Bavarian state premiershipImage: Heiko Becker/HMB-Media/IMAGO

blocks.text: Too much Bavaria in Berlin?

Germany has never had a president, or indeed a chancellor, from the CSU, a regional party that nevertheless wields national power thanks to its alliance with the CDU. One CSU man, Richard Stücklen, spent four years as president of the Bundestag — formally the country's second-highest office — from 1979.

If the door to the presidency does open for Aigner, many believe it would shut out Söder's ambitions to become chancellor. The CDU — a much bigger conservative party — usually overrules the CSU when it comes to choosing a chancellor candidate when the general election comes around, and it seems unlikely that the CDU would tolerate two CSU figures leading the country.

But Aigner's election would also remove one of Söder's key rivals back home: Aigner, still only 61, enjoys excellent popularity ratings and is considered a natural rival to the 59-year-old state premier.
Ultimately, by nominating Aigner, Merz is also paving the way for someone from the CDU to become the next chancellor — provided the CDU/CSU wins the next federal election, of course.
But first, the Federal Convention must make its decision on January 30. The new German president will officially assume office in mid-March.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Decoding report card ‘edu-ese’: Why parents are frustrated — and Alberta is getting involved
articles.summary: Alberta’s education minister has reopened the report card debate, proposing new legislation to make them more transparent for parents. Here’s what we learned by talking with parents and education…

image.caption: Schools across Alberta use a variety of descriptive terms in report cards rather than the traditional letter grades or percentages that parents might be used to. That's especially common at the elementary level and into junior high. (CBC)

blocks.text: Alberta’s education minister tapped into a big irritant for at least some parents when he said he’s taking on school report cards this year.

Today's report cards often use descriptive grading. Rather than giving students a percentage mark, or assigning a B or a C, many report cards in Alberta use words like “proficient” or “developing” to describe student progress. They lump all students into just a few categories, sometimes with numbers — one, two, three or four.
The descriptors are different across the province. They’re especially common at the elementary level, although descriptive grading can appear in junior high and high school, too.

Education experts say these descriptive report cards should actually make it easier for parents to follow how their kids are doing, but some parents say they’re frustrated with the jargon and really confused.
Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides said legislative changes will enable him to standardize report card requirements and bring more transparency for parents. (CBC)
Alberta Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides kicked off the debate again recently when he announced new legislation that he said will bring transparency and consistency across the province.
“That’s the primary driver behind these changes,” he said at a news conference. “We want to ensure that parents are receiving the most transparent information … as possible.”
He didn't say what new report cards will look like.
So, CBC News set out to understand how parents feel about report cards today.
Parents frustrated with ‘edu-ese,’ vague grading categories

Outside of Calgary’s West Ridge middle school at pickup time, we spoke with half a dozen parents who were frustrated with the fact that the Calgary Board of Education doesn’t use percentages until high school. Students get a one, two, three or four along with comments from their teacher.
“We're not sure whether two means pass or three means pass,” said Ieanne Yu, a parent who moved to Alberta from Hong Kong two years ago.
“The teacher’s comments are helpful but not deep enough,” added Fiona Tsang, whose daughter is with CBE in Grade 9.
“I don’t know if she’s at the high three, close to four. Or a low three, and she’s close to two.”

"It's too general. It works for kindergarten and early grades, but at Grade 6 they're still using this?" said Rafael Liao, a father of two boys in grades seven and two. "Of course, I can get more information at the one-on-one meeting with the teachers, but I expect to see more in the higher grades."

Fiona Tsang has a daughter in Grade 9 with the Calgary Board of Education. She finds the CBE four-point grade system makes it difficult to know how her daughter is doing academically. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
We did not hear the same frustration at Richmond elementary school, a short drive away. We spoke with half a dozen parents, and at those younger grades, all seemed happy with the system.

“I look at the number first. Then I see in the comments,” said Tanzia Hossain, whose daughter is in Grade 6. “The teacher knows if she needs any help, and [if I overlook something], they send me the email, always.”
After the school visits, we posted a call online, asking parents across the province for their thoughts on report cards.

One parent with children in two different Edmonton-based school boards wrote in to say their report cards are so full of “edu-ese,” she now runs all of the phrases through AI to get a plain language summary.
She’ll type: "What does 'analyze quantities to 1,000' mean in a Grade 2 Alberta report card?"

On the right, Ayaka Sakiki says she's happy with the report cards at Richmond School, and Rafael Liao says he'd like to see schools switch to percentages before junior high. On the left, Suderdeva Ganeshkumar says she's happy with the alternative reporting teachers give for her son, Dhakshean Ganeshkumar, and his learning challenges. (Elise Stolte and Nate Luit/CBC)
Another parent, Amber Dennison, questioned why report cards are now only online, which often requires parents to navigate complicated internet portals.
“Have you ever had to show a Grade 1 student their report card on a mobile phone? It means almost nothing to them,” she wrote. She hopes funding could support printing them.

But several other parents wrote to say they think the report cards are just fine. They worry the provincial announcement will only add stress for teachers, and report cards should be left with the school boards.

“I worry that it's a distraction from the lack of funding and the support of public education. I'm worried that it's another move to centralized power — taking power away from the boards and removing a layer of democracy,” said Hanita Simard.
She’s a Calgary-based parent who is both frustrated at recently introduced descriptive scales for CBE high school report cards and worried about the province getting too involved.
Education expert says descriptive grades encourage growth
So, why do schools use descriptive grading?

Shannon Ireland heads a non-profit consortium specifically focused on helping school boards improve assessment and report cards. She said descriptive report cards are part of a larger shift in how teachers assess student learning, called outcomes based assessment.

Her team encourages teachers to move away from the traditional model: teaching content, then testing students on it. Assessment should be more than a test, she said. Teachers should be assessing how students are learning through observing their work and having conversations with them, especially in the age of AI.

Report cards should communicate where a student is in their learning journey. And she says that can be communicated more clearly by saying, for example, that a child is at the beginning level or has mastered a task, than by giving the average of the percentage grades accumulated.
Shannon Ireland is a former classroom teacher and currently leads the Alberta Assessment Consortium. (Submitted by Shannon Ireland)

“I can understand parents being frustrated because there are a multitude of [descriptions] that we're seeing across the province. But what we're trying to help parents understand — that 75 per cent isn't as revealing as you think it might be. If your child gets 75 per cent in social studies, what does that actually tell you?" said Ireland.

“I think we're too quick to accept percentages in a school system. If you took your car to the mechanic and they said to you, 'Your car is operating at 75 per cent.' What does that mean? What's wrong with my car?”
The new approach is meant to describe how each child is doing in relation to each learning goal or outcome described in the curriculum, she said.
“It’s honouring the learning journey of every student,” she said. “It's about growth. It's a growth-based measure. Students know where they're at, where they need to go.”
Why is Alberta taking this on? Here’s one conservative take
Jeff Park is executive director of the Alberta Parents’ Union and travels across the province hosting conversations with parents.
He said when report cards come up, parents will say things like: “It turned out my kid had a problem with reading for three years before we actually understood it was a problem.”

Park thinks the issue is both confusing language, and teachers' reluctance to be direct and say what’s going wrong — because if comments need to be couched in the positive so that they are encouraging, many parents will simply miss that there are problems at all.
He said the Fraser Institute and Parents for Choice in Education have been advocating for change, and recently Alberta Education asked for some recommendations.
Jeff Park is the executive director of the Alberta Parents' Union. He says when parents are upset with report cards, it's often because they find them difficult to understand. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
“We were asked pretty much for a checklist, goodness, a year ago,” said Park. “Some of the biggest stuff is getting checked off.

“This is more of a school division issue, to be frank, but the buck stops at the provincial government. If school boards refuse to deal with something after parents have been telling them it's an issue for many, many years — as we have on this issue — then it's absolutely the domain of the provincial government to step in.”
This retired teacher believes she has a solution
Of course, teachers are also an important part of this conversation.

Earlier this year, CBC News surveyed more than 7,000 teachers about their classroom experience. When teachers brought up report cards, it was often in the context of being overwhelmed with classroom work already.

The report cards are taking up long days and evenings, outside of regularly scheduled work hours. Several teachers said they can see online how few parents even open the documents, and it feels like extra work when it repeats updates they file through PowerSchool and similar programs for parents continually.

Ann Bentley is a retired teacher from Edmonton who wrote in with her thoughts. In a phone call, she said she agrees there can be pressure for teachers to phrase things in positive terms, sometimes because parents react poorly to negative news.
But as for the language, she’s a fan of using descriptive terms instead of percentages. She says the real problem is that teachers often don’t know how to break out of the jargon.
“It's what they've been taught, what they learn. And they don't understand that parents aren't in the same boat.”
But there’s a solution at every school, she said: parent council.

“They exist in all school jurisdictions and within a school,” she said. “If there were some round tables so that there could be some consensus about what report card wording should be … so that they're more in layman's terms, that would be better.”

articles.title: Cat who hid in couch rescued from Saskatoon landfill
articles.summary: Moze the cat had enough lives to survive an unscheduled trip to the dump in her favourite hiding spot.

image.caption: Moze, a four-year-old cat, was reunited with her owner Ryan Nitschke after hiding in a couch that was taken to the Saskatoon landfill. (Submitted by Alisha Visser)

blocks.text: Saskatoon
Moze the cat had enough lives to survive an unscheduled trip to the dump in her favourite hiding spot.
'She is completely unharmed, unscathed and no injuries,' says owner of Moze, 4
A Saskatoon couple is happy their four-year-old cat, Moze, had enough of her nine lives left to survive an unexpected trip to the landfill inside her favourite hiding spot in a couch.
The ordeal started in October when Ryan Nitschke and Alisha Vessir had a couch and love seat moved out of their home to make space for new furniture.

“Like an hour later, my girlfriend and I were lying in bed and we were saying, ‘I wonder when Moze is going to reappear.’ She always hides whenever we have visitors. She hates company," Nitschke said. "Then it occurred to us that her favourite place is inside the couch.”
Moze, a four-year-old cat, was reunited with her owners after hiding in a couch and ending up in the Saskatoon landfill. (Submitted by Alisha Vessir)
In a panic, Nitschke got into the car and drove to the landfill.

“I explained the situation. We drove around and up to the top of the hill where they crush and compact the trash. Luckily, we didn't see any signs of the couches there. So we went down to the bins where it gets dropped off, and like, as we were driving up, they were hooking up the bin that had our couches.”
Matt Cuthbertson works at the material recovery centre. He said everything fell perfectly into place to find Moze.

“Normally I take a late lunch, which means I probably would have grabbed the full bins and taken them up top,” he said. “But I took an early lunch and when I was coming back, as I was hooking up to a bin, I heard over the radio, Johnny my manager, he’s like ‘don’t grab any bins. I’ll be right there.'”
LISTEN | Saskatoon Morning digs into Moze's rescue:
Saskatoon Morning6:30Moze the cat rescued moments before meeting a bulldozer at the landfill
Cuthbertson, who describes himself as a cat person, said it hit home.
“When I initially heard this, my stomach dropped, and I was pretty devastated. But also that adrenaline of like, if it’s here, we've got to find this cat,” he said.
The crew found Nitscke’s furniture in the bin and began cutting into the couches.
Cuthbertson said they didn’t see any sign of Moze at first, but kept going.
“We're fiddling around, kind of looking for every nook and cranny,” he said. “All of a sudden, yeah, Johnny's like, 'I see it.'”
Moze was curled up inside the couch's armrest. All the workers could see was belly, fur and eyes.
“Perfect happy ending. The fact that we didn’t give up after, and Johnny’s eagle eyes, he saved us. I just felt this joy," Cuthbertson said. "It was a beautiful thing.”
How this Sask. cat accidentally took a trip to the dump
Nitschke is amazed that everything turned out so well and thankful that everyone at the landfill went the extra mile to help.
“There were so many opportunities for the worst to happen. But she is completely unharmed, unscathed and no injuries,” Nitschke said.
"She was a little scared when she got home, but by the end of the night she was back to her usual self."
A thank you note for the landfill crew who helped rescue Moze. (Submitted by the City of Saskatoon)
With files from Chelsea Cross

articles.title: Deadly floods hit Iraq as thunderstorms sweep across region
articles.summary:
Violent storms lash northern Iraq and parts of Iran, while Portugal faces strong winds and Japan braces for further snowfall

Deadly flash floods hit northern Iraq on Saturday as severe…
articles.byline: Oliver Wyndham-Lewis and Magdalena Shopova for the MetDesk

blocks.text: Deadly flash floods hit northern Iraq on Saturday as severe thunderstorms swept across the region, including in neighbouring Iran. The city of Erbil, in Iraq, was particularly badly hit, with extensive damage to homes and businesses. Streets were inundated as torrential rain fell over a short period.
Rainfall exceeded forecasts, with an estimated 80mm falling in the city, compared with expectations of 30mm. Two people were killed in the floods.

In Europe, Storm Bruna is forecast to bring strong winds to Portugal this week, particularly along the west coast. Gusts are expected to reach 50mph (80km/h), with heavy rain and thunderstorms also expected. The total rainfall could reach 200mm by the end of the week. The storm has already affected the Canary Islands, where Tenerife recorded a gust of 80mph on Saturday night.
Japan experienced a cold and snowy end to last week, with further snowfall expected in Hokkaido and parts of the mountains in the main island Honshu.

Temperatures in Japan are forecast to fall below the seasonal average early this week, with Sapporo, the capital of Hokkaido prefecture, expected to plunge to 10C below average. Maximum temperatures in the city are likely to be about 4-6C on Monday and Wednesday, while Tuesday’s high is forecast to be about 0C. Minimum temperatures could fall to -6C by Wednesday, and -8C in other western parts of Hokkaido on Tuesday.
Ski resorts are preparing for visitors after snowfall began on Friday. Total snowfall is expected to reach 30-50cm around Kiroro and Niesko, with about 20-30cm in Furano, Rusutsu and Sapporo.
Other resorts could receive up to 20cm of snow by Wednesday. Strong winds accompanied the snow on Friday and over the weekend, with gusts of about 75mph in Kiroko and Niesko.

During the strong El Niño, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific were about 3.5C above the climatological average at their peak in late October. As a result, Peru has been experiencing air temperatures 5-10C above the seasonal average. The unusually warm conditions expected to continue into next week.

articles.title: Less time perfecting the shot, more time living in the moment: Putting the vivo V80 to the test
articles.summary: Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by vivo and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler.

blocks.text: Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by vivo and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Our generation has been told countless times that we don’t know how to live in the moment. We’ve been criticized for being too immersed in our phones — more concerned with capturing the perfect moment than enjoying what’s happening right in front of us.

But for a generation of digital natives, the two aren’t necessarily mutually exclusive. We can be fully present in an experience and still want something to remember it by. In fact, our camera rolls have become something of a personal diary — filled with moments that mean a lot to us.
And years later, when these photos resurface, it’s rarely just about remembering what happened, but about how we felt at that particular point in our lives.
So naturally, we’d want a phone that makes doing both easier. Something that makes capturing beautiful moments effortless, without compromising on style or everyday functionality.

Equipped with a ZEISS camera system, AI-powered photography features, and a customizable OriginOS 7 interface, the vivo V80 promises to make taking beautiful photos a little less complicated. So we took it out for a stroll to see just how much easier documenting everyday life could actually get.
At 85mm, the camera captured lovely portraits while keeping some of the surroundings in the frame.
At 100mm, I actually expected the photo to lose some sharpness already, but I was pleasantly surprised by how crisp it still turned out.
We also tested the vivo V80’s zoom capabilities, taking the same photo at 1x, 3x, and 10x while standing in the same spot.
At 1x, we captured the entire street, while 3x brought the buildings closer without losing much detail. Even at 10x, we were surprised by how clearly the architectural details came through.
This could be useful at concerts and live shows, where you want to take good photos or videos despite the distance and often unpredictable stage lighting.
Another feature we had fun experimenting with was the vivo V80’s AI Creative Camera.
Take these photos, for example. An afternoon stroll around Salcedo Village looked like springtime in Japan. It’s obviously not how the place looks in real life — but that’s the fun of it.

blocks.caption: SALCEDO VILLAGE, JAPAN? Trying out ‘Travel’ filters on the vivo V80’s AI Creative Camera feature.

blocks.text: This is a photo we shot using the Top Lighting feature. It’s best for when you want a studio-like look even without professional lighting tools.

We also tried the default 50mm setting of the main camera for a candid shot, and I love how the photo turned out even without posing too much (lol). The colors looked natural and vibrant, with the trees and greenery appearing crisp and detailed even in the wider shot.

Another fun feature of the vivo V80 is the Creative Sticker Collage, which lets you turn your photos into personalized layouts. It’s a nice touch for creatives who want to do a little more with their photos. I tested it out using shots of vivo brand ambassador Anne Curtis from the launch.
Another feature I enjoyed exploring was OriginOS 7’s customizable themes. There are four to choose from: Wiggle, Pet Pals, Glint, and StickIt.

I tried the Pet Pals theme, which gives you an adorable virtual pet right on your lock screen. You can even set its waking times, making it feel like your very own digital Tamagotchi! It’s a playful detail that makes interacting with your phone a lot more fun.

One thing that genuinely surprised me was how fast the vivo V80 charges. I walked into a café with my battery at 0%, plugged it in, and when I checked again just 15 minutes later, it was already at 49%! Honestly, I couldn’t believe it. Its 90W FlashCharge is definitely a feature I’d appreciate on particularly busy days.

The vivo V80’s Starwish Purple variant is particularly pretty in person. Its galaxy-inspired design has a subtle shimmer that changes depending on how the light hits it. It’s perfect for people who love aesthetically pleasing things.
Ready to make the upgrade?

articles.title: Four killed in Gaza after sand embankment collapses onto tents, health ministry says
articles.summary: Three children are among those killed in the incident that came a day after heavy rain reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza.

blocks.text: Three children and one woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in central Gaza following heavy rain, the Hamas-run health ministry says.
Five injured people were also reportedly rescued after the incident on Sunday night at a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah.
Videos showed men using phone torches to search for survivors beneath boulders, sand and collapsed tents.

The Civil Defence service, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said the "humanitarian tragedy" should prompt urgent action by international organisations to provide safe shelters for displaced people and move tents away from sandy areas, slopes and locations at risk of collapse.
Torrential rain on Saturday reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, leaving many Palestinians without a dry place to sleep.
The Civil Defence said water levels reached up to 1.5m (4.9ft) in some places and that its first responders were able to respond to only 10% of the 2,100 distress calls they received.
"Protecting the lives of displaced people is an urgent humanitarian responsibility. Their tents must not become death traps beneath sand and rainwater," it warned.

The Civil Defence initially reported on Sunday that three children and two women were killed when the sand embankment collapsed. But the health ministry said on Monday morning that only one woman was among the dead.
She was identified as Tahrir Nabhan, while the children were named as Mariam Nabhan and her brother Salah, and Habiba al-Zein.
Mustafa al-Masri told the BBC that he and other rescuers had used their bare hands to dig the victims and survivors out of the sand and rubble.
"It was extremely difficult. This mound was huge and wide. It collapsed onto the tent, and we didn't know what to do," he said.
"When we got here, we, along with the young men from the camp, pulled them out with our own hands. We pulled out the children and the woman."
"Their father arrived shouting, 'My children, my children, my children, my children.' We pulled his children out, put them in the ambulance, and took them to the hospital."
Masri added that he had been displaced from the northern town of Beit Hanoun but had stayed in central Gaza because there was "nowhere for me to return to".
"We went out looking around, searching through the open areas and hills, but I couldn't find any place other than this area that felt suitable for me."

The International Organization for Migration's regional crisis co-ordinator, Karl Baker, told the BBC from Gaza that the territory's 2.1 million population was confined to only 30% of its total area and that many people were "unfortunately living in areas which would not be normal if we were not in this time of conflict".
He said the UN agency and its partners were trying to make sure there were enough tents and tarpaulins, as well as improved drainage in camps, to help them get through the winter.
However, he warned that aid currently getting into Gaza was not sufficient to meet the demands of the population, describing it as "the very smallest of Band-Aids [plasters]".
"We need more support, in-kind donations. We need funding in order to help the communities to help themselves," he said. "We need a lot more to happen."
UN agencies have called on Israeli authorities to allow in the specialist equipment and materials required to improve living conditions for displaced families.

Cogat, the Israeli military body tasked with co-ordinating deliveries, said on Sunday that more than 91,000 tents, 12 vacuum trucks for waste removal, and fuel and engine oil for pumping facilities have been delivered since the start of the "Gaza Winterization Plan".
But it added that Israel would not permit the entry of equipment that could be used for military purposes by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups.
An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.
More than 1.9 million people have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.

The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed in October 2025, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,640 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Additional reporting by Malak Hassouneh

articles.title: Pangilinan, De Lima still hopeful Robedo will seek presidency anew in 2028
articles.summary: Allies of former Vice President Leni Robredo remain hopeful that she will change her mind about a second presidential run in 2028.

blocks.text: Published November 9, 2026 6:11pm
Allies of former Vice President Leni Robredo remain hopeful that she will change her mind about a second presidential run in 2028.

On Monday, House Senior Deputy Minority Leader Leila de Lima of ML party-list and and Senator Francis Pangilinan made the comments after Robredo said earlier in the day that she won’t pursue a 2028 presidential bid but would rather support a deserving presidential candidate.

“I find it very regrettable to hear that it is as if she has made up her mind. But you know, hope runs eternal. We continue to hope….we continue to hope na baka naman may [that there is still a] chance pa na magbago ang isip niya [that she will change her mind],” De Lima told reporters.

“Whatever her final decision we're going to respect that. But we're still keeping our fingers crossed. We're still hoping that she will change her mind. We in the LP are yet to talk about this but I am sure that we share the same sentiments [of wanting her to run]. Umaasa talaga akong magbabago ang kanyang desisyon [I am really hoping she will change her decision]. She is the best hope for our country,” De Lima added.

De Lima said that with the filing of candidacy set around last week of September to first week of October next year, Robredo can still reopen that door to a second presidential run and make a decision by first quarter of January 2028.

“Ayaw ko maniwala na talagang tuldok na tuldok na iyong pagkakasara [ng pinto]…ng kanyang desisyon. Personally, ayaw kong tanggapin pa yan at this point. Because I do believe na kailangan talaga siya ng bansa,” she said.
[I don't want to believe that she has closed the door. Personally, I don't want to believe that at this point. I do believe our country needs her.]

“With all of the problems, with all of the issues, with all of the challenges in our country and our political climate is facing right now…ang kailangan natin na somebody like VP Leni. She has proven competence and integrity to implement good governance,” she added.
Robredo ran for president in 2022 but lost against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Robredo got 14 million votes as against Marcos' 31 million.

Senator Pangilinan, for his part, harked back to 26 years when then-Senator Benigno Aquino III also had no plans to run for president but later on went on to be the standard bearer of the opposition for the 2010 polls.
Aquino eventually won the 2010 presidential polls.

“Si dating Pangulong Noynoy nung senador pa sya ay wala ring planong tumakbong presidente. Tinutulan din nya yung unang panawagan ng taumbayn na tumakbo siya sa 2010 pero sa huling banda hindi na siya maka hindi dahil taumbayan na ang nagpasiya at nagsabi na dapat siya tumakbo,” Pangilinan said.
(President Noynoy also had no plans to run for President and turned down offers for him to run. But ultimately, he cannot refuse the call of the people who wanted him to be president.)
“Sa 2028, naniniwala ako na taumbayan din ang magpapasiya at magtatagumpay para sa bayan,” he added.
(For 2028, I am also of the belief that the people’s will is the ultimate decider.) — RSJ, GMA News
